POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Wed, 21 Oct 2026 16:01:48 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Perquisitions au Parlement européen dans une enquête visant l’ancien groupe du RN https://www.politico.eu/article/perquisitions-au-parlement-europeen-dans-une-enquete-visant-ancien-groupe-du-rn/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 21 Oct 2026 15:36:08 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9199862 STRASBOURG — Des agents sous l’autorité du Parquet européen ont procédé mercredi matin à une perquisition dans les bureaux des équipes du groupe d’extrême droite des Patriotes au Parlement européen.

Ces perquisitions s’inscrivent dans le cadre d’une enquête portant sur des soupçons d’irrégularités dans l’utilisation de fonds européens et visant l’ancien groupe Identité et démocratie (ID). En 2025, le service financier du Parlement a constaté que ce dernier avait dépensé 4,3 millions d’euros entre 2019 et 2024 en dons et appels d’offres irréguliers. Le Parquet européen, chargé d’enquêter sur les infractions financières portant atteinte au budget de l’Union européenne, a ouvert une enquête sur la base des rapports du Parlement.

“Depuis ce matin, des perquisitions sont en cours au sein du Parlement européen à Strasbourg, où nous nous trouvons, visant les bureaux des collaborateurs de l’ancien groupe Identité et démocratie”, a relaté sur X Jean-Paul Garraud, président de la délégation des députés européens du RN.

Les perquisitions ont eu lieu dans les bureaux du secrétariat général du groupe, selon deux responsables qui ont souhaité garder l’anonymat pour s’exprimer au sujet de l’enquête en cours.

Lorsqu’ID a été dissous en 2024, bon nombre de ses membres ont rejoint les Patriotes, notamment des élus du Rassemblement national, du Parti de la liberté d’Autriche (FPÖ), du Fidesz hongrois, du Vlaams Belang (Intérêt flamand) belge, de l’ANO 2011 tchèque et du parti espagnol Vox.

Dans un communiqué, les Patriotes insistent sur le fait qu’il n’existe “aucune continuité juridique” avec le groupe ID, et qu’ils “ne sont pas visés” par les perquisitions.

Les soupçons portent sur l’utilisation du budget alloué chaque année par le Parlement européen aux groupes politiques pour couvrir leurs frais administratifs et opérationnels. Le Parquet européen enquête pour déterminer si le groupe ID a versé des dons irréguliers à des organisations régionales dans plusieurs pays de l’Union européenne, et s’il a enfreint les règles relatives aux appels d’offres dans le cadre de contrats attribués à des entreprises proches du groupe.

En 2025, le service financier a ordonné aux Patriotes de restituer 276 967 euros de fonds européens qui, selon lui, auraient été indûment dépensés au cours du second semestre 2024, dans le cadre de procédures d’appel d’offres irrégulières similaires.

“Comme toujours lorsqu’on le lui demande, le Parlement coopère avec les autorités compétentes. Nous n’avons pas d’autres commentaires à faire”, a déclaré un porte-parole du Parlement européen dans un SMS.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Britain’s new prime minister has promised greater “public control” of the water industry as a centerpiece of his domestic agenda, partly reversing a wave of privatization that began in the 1980s. Ministers are due to unveil more detail in a “10-year plan for Britain” that is currently expected in December.

However, while this 10-year plan will contain a high-level vision, priorities and principles for the industry’s future, much of the granular detail of how future ownership models will work in practice is only expected later, said two people with knowledge of the discussions.

Some of these key details will be laid out in Chancellor John Healey’s multi-year spending review at some point in 2027, added the two people, who were granted anonymity to discuss evolving policy. One said the spending review — a date for which has not been decided — was where the full details would be “nailed down.”

These include any fiscal implications for the Treasury, which could have to find billions of pounds if ministers decided to transfer privately-owned shares to the public purse.

This appears to mirror an approach Burnham has taken to policymaking for decades, first as a Cabinet minister and then mayor of Greater Manchester before he took over 10 Downing Street in July. He is known for setting out a broad direction which his officials can later use to pin down detailed policy, while also seeking buy-in from private industry.

With a general election due by summer 2029, however, any wait will compress the prime minister’s window to enact far-reaching reform before he goes back to the electorate.

‘£40 being added to every single water bill’

England’s privatized water firms also argue that uncertainty over the sector’s future is damaging investor confidence.

The industry trade association Water UK has said the entire industry risks being downgraded by the credit ratings agency Moody’s, which would add £40 to customers’ annual bills.

Water UK Chief Executive David Henderson urged the government to move ahead with reforms suggested last year by former Bank of England Deputy Governor Jon Cunliffe, before ministers decide the overall path of how the sector is owned.

The Cunliffe report “was given to the government 15 months ago and the credit rating agencies are watching,” Henderson told POLITICO. “If the government doesn’t pretty soon decide what it wants to do with that report, then we risk a downgrade, as Moody’s has indicated. And if there’s a downgrade, that would sadly see £40 being added to every single water bill across England and Wales. That’s the last thing anybody wants.”

He added: “We still have no idea how [a proposed] new regulator will look, what status it will have, what its duties will be, which parts of the Environment Agency will stay in the Environment Agency, and which parts will go into the new regulator. That is causing uncertainty … an important consideration for any investor.”

One government official insisted the 10-year plan would contain some finer details of plans to overhaul the water industry, though they accepted that fiscal implications were always dealt with in fiscal events such as the spending review. 

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is also due to bring a water bill to parliament before Christmas with separate policy, such as closing what Burnham has called “loopholes used to pay excessive bonuses” to water company executives. It will also contain scrutiny powers for regional mayors.

Burnham announced last month that the bill would lift a ban on the government owning more than 3% of shares in any English water firm. But he has also long made clear that he would not fully nationalize the industry, a move the government previously estimated would cost £100 billion for England and Wales together.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh, one of Burnham’s most powerful allies in government, is leading three task forces including one on public control of water alongside housing, energy and transport.

Officials have been working through a “spectrum of options” for how public control in the water sector will look, a second government official said. They added that ministers are due to begin deciding which option — or combination of options — will be taken forward before the 10-year plan.

]]> fr Prosecutor searches far-right group offices in EU Parliament https://www.politico.eu/article/patriots-european-parliament-office-search-eu-funds-mismanagement/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 21 Oct 2026 13:52:02 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9199184 STRASBOURG — Officials acting on behalf of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office searched the offices of staff of the far-right Patriots group in the European Parliament on Wednesday morning.

The searches are part of an investigation into allegations that the now-defunct Identity and Democracy group mismanaged EU funds. In 2025, the Parliament’s finance department found that ID misspent €4.3 million between 2019 and 2024 in irregular donations and public tenders. The EPPO, which investigates financial crimes involving the EU budget, opened a probe based on the Parliament’s reports. 

“Since this morning, searches have been underway at the European Parliament in Strasbourg — where we are currently located — targeting the offices of staff members of the former Identity and Democracy Group,” said France’s National Rally chief in the Parliament, Jean-Paul Garraud. 

The EPPO confirmed it carried out searches in the Parliament’s buildings in France and Belgium “as part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European funds by a former political group in the European Parliament.”

The searches took place at the group’s secretariat offices, according to two officials, granted anonymity to speak about the ongoing investigation.

When ID dissolved in 2024, many of its staff moved to the Patriots, including lawmakers from France’s National Rally, Austria’s Freedom Party, Hungary’s Fidesz, Spain’s Vox, Belgium’s Flemish Interest and Czechia’s ANO 2011.

In their statement, the group insisted “there is no legal continuity with the ID Group” and that “it is not involved in the ongoing investigations.”

The allegations of mismanagement of funds relate to the budget allocated annually by the Parliament for political groups to spend on administrative and operative costs. EPPO is probing whether ID made irregular donations to regional organizations in several EU countries, and whether the group breached tender rules in contracts awarded to companies friendly to the group.

In 2025, the finance department ordered the Patriots to give back €276,967 in EU funds it says the group misused during the second half of 2024, related to similar irregular tender procedures.

“As always when requested Parliament cooperates with relevant authorities — we don’t have additional comment,” a Parliament spokesperson said via a text message.

]]> en Publishers want Brussels and London to stop Meta’s new AI terms https://www.politico.eu/article/publishers-press-brussels-and-london-to-stop-metas-new-ai-terms/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 21 Oct 2026 13:23:02 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9199001 BRUSSELS — Europe’s biggest media companies have asked regulators in Brussels and London to stop Meta from introducing new terms they say would let it copy publishers’ websites to build artificial intelligence, as a backlash that began in the U.S. spreads across Europe.

In a letter Monday, the European Publishers Council, whose members include POLITICO’s owner Axel Springer, called on EU competition boss Teresa Ribera and tech chief Henna Virkkunen to press Meta to put the terms on hold before they take effect Oct. 30.

The group wants Brussels to check them against EU copyright and competition law, and has requested an urgent meeting with the teams of both commissioners.

“The Commission remains committed to ensure that Meta’s practices fully comply with all applicable obligations under EU law, including competition rules and the Digital Markets Act,” Commission spokesperson Ricardo Cardoso told POLITICO, referring to the EU’s rulebook for Big Tech. He said Brussels was aware of both Meta’s changes and publishers’ concerns.

The U.K. competition watchdog has moved as well. British publishers have complained to the Competition and Markets Authority that Meta is so dominant they are compelled to accept its terms. 

The watchdog’s chief, Sarah Cardell, told British lawmakers on Tuesday that it had asked Meta to explain the changes and would meet the company on Wednesday. She named Meta as a possible candidate for Britain’s new rules for tech giants.

The terms cover businesses that use Meta’s tools to run Facebook pages, Instagram accounts or ads, which includes almost every newsroom. 

The fight began in the U.S. last week, when Nieman Lab, a journalism research outlet at Harvard, reported on the terms after receiving a tip from a small business owner.

As first written, they let Meta send automated programs to copy websites linked to those accounts and use the material to “train” its products, Nieman Lab concluded. There is no opt-out, and a business that continues to use Meta’s tools after Oct. 30 will be deemed to have consented.

Publishers say the terms would hand Meta content for free that other AI companies pay to license.

Rapid reaction

On Friday, Meta communications chief Andy Stone responded on X that the Nieman Lab report was “false” and that there was “no change to how Meta uses web crawlers.”

Stone said the update aimed to let Meta pull accurate product information from shopping sites for ads, not to scrape news sites. The company also said the crawling language already existed in other Meta terms and was just being gathered in one place.

Late Friday, however, Meta revised the terms and deleted the word “train,” saying the terms cover only its advertising and business products.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify,” a spokesperson for Meta told POLITICO over the weekend, adding the change was “not about scraping news sites.”

Publishers say that changes little, however. 

Meta has given them verbal assurances that they can keep using its tools without surrendering their content to AI, but the terms themselves don’t guarantee that, the European Publishers Council’s letter says.

“Meta’s supposed Friday night correction is a farce,” said Jason Kint, who heads Digital Content Next, a U.S. publisher group whose members include Axel Springer. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.”

Others have gone further. 

“This is unscrupulous theft,” Germany’s newspaper and magazine associations said in a joint statement on Tuesday. They want Brussels to block the terms while it reviews them, warning that once articles are copied into AI systems, they can’t be clawed back.

Joseph Bambridge in London contributed reporting.

]]> en Macron slams ‘stupid’ comments after Trump pins French riots on immigration https://www.politico.eu/article/macron-slams-unacceptable-and-stupid-comments-after-trump-pins-french-riots-on-immigration/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 21 Oct 2026 11:35:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9198245 PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday hit out at the “unacceptable and stupid comments from many foreign leaders” in the aftermath of unrest which rocked several French cities over the weekend.

“Some people have claimed that we’ve been overrun by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron told reporters during a trip to Qatar. His comments were a clear swipe at U.S. President Donald Trump, who this week railed that France is “being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and Communists.”

While hundreds of thousands of protesters in France demonstrated peacefully over the cost of living and school conditions at the weekend, the mayhem — including public buildings being set on fire, stores being looted and clashes with riot police — sparked widespread condemnation in France and abroad, including in the U.S., where Trump is using the French unrest to rally voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.

There is no evidence tying last weekend’s incidents in France to immigration.

Macron said Trump is “among” a group of political leaders who are campaigning “off of France’s back,” adding, “it’s at times like these that you can tell who loves France and who doesn’t.”

Right-leaning leaders in other European countries like Hungary and Poland also tried to pin the unrest in France on immigration to justify their countries’ hard-line policies on the divisive issue. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on X that the chaos that engulfed several French cities makes it “clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration.”

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot responded by offering to “assist the countries concerned in understanding the situation, to prevent them from spreading or relaying false information.”

“Foreign leaders who comment on or exploit recent events in France for electoral purposes or to harm us — without understanding anything about them — should show at least a basic measure of restraint,” he added.

]]> en Suspicious drones spotted flying over French military sites https://www.politico.eu/article/suspicious-drone-fly-over-france-military-site/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 21 Oct 2026 11:03:13 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9197993 PARIS — Suspicious drones flew over military facilities in southeastern France earlier this month, the French navy said on Wednesday.

During a large-scale armed forces exercise that lasted from Oct. 5 to Oct. 16, “unauthorized drones were detected in the no-fly zone, near and above military sites,” the navy said in a press statement.

“In each instance, the planned security measures were activated by the deployment of anti-drone devices, in coordination with domestic security forces,” it continued, adding that a judicial investigation was opened.

Suspicious drones are increasingly spotted in several European countries including Denmark, Germany and France, close to military sites and defense industry facilities. In July, a Moldovan man was arrested on suspicion of espionage after flying an unmanned aerial vehicle over a KNDS factory in Munich. Some of these drone incursions are attributed to Russia, as Moscow intensifies its hybrid attacks against European countries.

The French navy’s statement confirms local media reporting about drone sightings around Toulon. The southeastern town is home to one of France’s largest naval bases, which hosts the country’s aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle as well as attack submarines.

According to local broadcaster Ici Provence, the drones flew at night above the naval base, the General Directorate of Armaments facility in Toulon, and the 54th Artillery Regiment in Hyères. The military exercise, dubbed Typhon, was precisely aimed at training against drone sightings.

The navy said that no sensitive infrastructure was threatened. “The Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs reminds the public that unauthorized drone flights near or over military facilities are strictly prohibited,” the statement concluded.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Wed, 21 Oct 2026 15:45:40 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 EU looks to UK, Canada, and Japan to plug €70bn hole in funding for Ukraine’s 2027 war effort https://euobserver.com/244118/eu-looks-to-uk-canada-and-japan-to-plug-e70bn-hole-in-funding-for-ukraines-2027-war-effort/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 15:45:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244118 The EU is pressing allies, such as the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway to help close a €70bn shortfall in Ukraine’s funding for next year.]]> The EU is pressing allies, such as the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway, to help close a €70bn shortfall in Ukraine’s funding for next year, after president Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the war will cost €155bn in 2027.

EU Council president António Costa told MEPs in Strasbourg on Wednesday (21 October) that member states already provided 80 percent of external aid to Ukraine and “international partners must also step up their efforts”. 

“Our commitment to peace must go hand in hand with sustained pressure on the aggressor,” he also said, after meeting Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels last week.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen also told MEPs on Wednesday: “The war will not be decided on the frontline; the war will be decided in our political will, in whether we stand up for freedom and democracy and support our Ukrainian friends.” 

Zelensky’s €155bn figure refers to Ukraine’s total war-related spending in 2027, part of which Kyiv covers from its own budget.

But that still left a €70bn gap that Ukraine needed foreign partners to fill, as next year approached.

The EU has already agreed a €90bn loan covering 2026 and 2027, meant to meet two-thirds of Ukraine’s financing needs over that period.

The remaining third was supposed to come from other partners, but so far that money has been secured only for 2026, not for 2027.

Read more

EU commits €3.3bn to Ukrainian drones as funding gap remains unresolved ahead of ‘tough winter’

Costa told MEPs on Wednesday that €16bn had been disbursed this year under the defence line of the loan, while another €17bn could be sent to Ukraine if anti-corruption reforms were implemented.

“Our determination to support Ukraine and its people is stronger than ever,” he said.

EU hopes for Ukraine cash from allies

Meanwhile, EU commissioner Maroš Šefčovič also indicated on Monday that Britain will be asked to increase funding to Ukraine, speaking ahead of an EU-UK summit on 20 November.

“Following the signature of a contribution agreement on 13 July 2026, the UK can now participate under the EU’s €90bn Ukraine support loan,” he said.

Both the EU and UK would support Ukraine “as long as it takes to bring Russia’s illegal war of aggression to an end”, Šefčovič added.

    ]]>         Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate https://euobserver.com/243936/europes-youth-asked-for-hope-but-politicians-just-offer-fear-and-hate/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 10:24:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243936 As Europe pours billions into defence and talks up ‘strategic autonomy’, it is quietly undermining its own power by ignoring the students who say they can’t afford the education, housing or stability needed to keep the continent running.]]> Student protests across Europe are a desperate cry for help, an appeal to governments to build a brighter, hope-filled future. Instead of paying attention, European politicians have decided to manhandle the protesters, misrepresent their demands and manipulate public opinion.

    Different narratives are now competing to explain what the protests are really about.

    They want to be taught properly. They want more teachers, an end to overcrowded classes, dilapidated buildings and inadequate school meals and an admissions system that sorts young people by class and postcode.

    In Belgium, students have protested education cuts and fees. Greek students occupied Syntagma Square over rents, student housing and energy bills. Italian students demanded money for schools rather than war.

    Read more

    Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting

    But politicians seem intent on telling a different story.

    For many EU leaders it is – yet again – all about migration.

    Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar has decided that the chaos in French cities makes it “clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration.”

    Poland’s Donald Tusk, who insists he will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, joined the leaders of Denmark and Italy at the EU leaders’ meeting in Brussels last week to push for an even tougher Fortress Europe.

    Together, they almost succeeded in getting others in the EU to agree to a statement linking crime and “irregular” migration.

    On the other side of the Atlantic, US president Donald Trump instructed Europe to “close your borders and take control, before it is too late!” while his deputy JD Vance criticised Western liberals for bringing the “third world” to France.

    Parts of the media focused on the violence, particularly the looting and destruction carried out by those who have joined the protests to create chaos, rather than on the demands that brought students onto the streets in the first place.

    In France, meanwhile, it was the presidential campaign that shaped the political response, with Marine Le Pen from the National Rally calling for law and order and blaming “decades of immigration” for the violence while her protégé, Jordan Bardella, said the police should have more weapons and greater powers.

    Read more

    Can the EU survive with far-right leaders running major member states? The answer is worrying

    Jean-Luc Mélenchon of France Insoumise, Le Pen’s leading rival in the elections next year, was accused of fuelling student anger. French centrists struggled to find their footing and their voice. President Emmanuel Macron made an angry television appearance before heading to the Middle East with a delegation of business leaders.

    So far, very predictable.

    Old playbook: one enemy, no solution

    Divert, distract, dehumanise and scapegoat are the oldest tricks in wily politicians’ playbook. The well-worn recipe is simple: take a social crisis, remove its economic content, replace it with a face, a religion, a border. Then offer an enemy, not a solution.

    When public services fail, blame the outsider. When wages stagnate, blame the foreigner. When housing becomes impossible, blame the newcomer rather than the landlord, the investor or the government that stopped building.

    And when young people take to the streets, describe them as manipulated, criminal, alien or dangerous. Treat their anger as a threat to public order rather than a warning that something is profoundly wrong. Say there has been foreign manipulation and disinformation.

    Then turn the full force of the state against the symptoms of the crisis while leaving its causes untouched and change the the subject from justice to fear, from schools to borders, from the future to the past.

    Meanwhile, the money goes elsewhere.

    Europe is pouring resources into defence and rearmament. Governments speak endlessly of competitiveness, productivity and strategic autonomy. But these questions cannot become excuses for neglecting the social foundations on which Europe’s future depends.

    Seriously, who is going to make an ageing Europe competitive if the people expected to build its future cannot afford to have one? Who will run Europe’s basic services if migrants go “home”? What does strategic autonomy even mean if young Europeans cannot get a decent education, find secure employment or afford a home?

    Contradictions

    We should know by now that security cannot be measured in weapons alone. It also depends on how secure citizens feel, and whether they believe they have something worth protecting. Security demands that people have politicians they can trust and institutions which work for them.

    A Europe that invests in its military capabilities while allowing its schools, housing systems and public services to deteriorate risks hollowing out its own strength.

    Believe me: I know. I was born in Pakistan, a country which thrives on war and conflict and neglects the well being of its citizens.

    There is another contradiction. As young people struggle to make their voices heard, the EU is planning cuts to funding for civil society organisations that defend rights, support communities, hold power to account and help turn public anger into democratic participation.

    The EU has always – rightly – backed citizens’ calls for democratic participation, equality and inclusion when it happens in Tunisia, Egypt or Hongkong. How can our leaders close down such calls for participation when they are made at home?

    Sadly, politicians and parts of the media have lost young peoples’ trust – and when that faith goes, so does democracy.

    The EU can and must offer young Europeans a story of hope, inclusion and progress towards equality. Leaders who prefer to hallucinate about migrants should spend more time living up to the EU’s values by investing in education, affordable housing, decent jobs and public services.

    We must give our young people a meaningful voice in decisions that will shape their lives. Our collective future quite literally depends on it.

    ]]>         ‘I’m 42 and I’ve spent my entire adult life held captive by Bibi’ – can Israel finally break free of Netanyahu, as Hungary did of Orbán? https://euobserver.com/243796/im-42-and-ive-spent-my-entire-adult-life-held-captive-by-bibi-can-israel-finally-break-free-of-netanyahu-as-hungary-did-of-orban/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 09:15:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243796 Benjamin Netanyahu has not been Israel’s prime minister for every one of those years. Yet even out of office, Israeli politics rarely escaped his gravitational pull. Hungarians know something about that feeling.]]> Over coffee, an Israeli woman I know began to cry. “I’m 42,” she said, “and I’ve spent my entire adult life held captive by Bibi.”

    Benjamin Netanyahu has not been Israel’s prime minister for every one of those years. Yet even out of office, Israeli politics rarely escaped his gravitational pull.

    For him or against him, public life kept arranging itself around his presence.

    Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having previously held office from 1996 to 1999 and from 2009 to 2021, and from 2022 onward.

    Hungarians know something about that feeling. For 16 years, Viktor Orbán was not merely Hungary’s prime minister but the organising fact of Hungarian politics. Institutions bent around him, opponents defined themselves against him, and arguments somehow ended up being about him.

    On 12 April, that era ended.

    Péter Magyar’s insurgent Tisza party defeated Fidesz after 16 uninterrupted years in power. The final results gave Tisza 141 of parliament’s 199 seats, a two-thirds majority.

    The temptation is to tell a simple story of liberation: the dominant leader fell, the spell broke, democracy returned. But political systems leave habits behind, and Orbán’s most durable legacy may prove to be the way Hungarians learned to imagine politics itself.

    That is also Magyar’s dilemma.

    Opposition movements confronting personalised systems often conclude that they, too, need a protagonist capable of gathering diffuse grievances into a political force.

    Yet the qualities that help an insurgency win are not necessarily those needed to build a pluralist order afterwards. Campaigns reward concentration, and democracy depends on dispersing authority.

    A challenger may have to become indispensable in order to win. Governing democratically requires eventually proving that he is not.

    For people my age, Orbán’s rise was a rupture because we remember other governments and possibilities. Many of my students, now in their 20s, do not. Their political adulthood unfolded almost entirely under Fidesz. Orbán was simply there, as unavoidable as the weather.

    Power can come to look distant and durable, participation noble but futile, and institutions captured or irrelevant. Politics becomes something done to you rather than something you do.

    Read more

    Hungary’s conundrum: undoing Orbán – without becoming Orbán 

    Conversations with Orbán

    I know how deeply that can lodge itself in the mind. For five years, I have had countless conversations with Orbán in which I argued with him and tried to persuade him to change course. All of them took place in my dreams.

    Supporters and opponents experienced Orbán’s system differently, but both learned to orient themselves around the same centre of gravity. Loyalists read its signals, while critics watched it constantly and defined themselves against it.

    Parties that spend years confronting a dominant machine tend to centralise themselves. Message discipline becomes existential, disagreement can look like sabotage, and restraint like something to discuss after victory.

    That is why Hungary’s challenge is larger than reversing Orbán’s policies.

    A government elected to repair democratic institutions has to accept restraints precisely when it can most easily avoid them: strengthening parliament even when it dominates it, protecting independent media when they attack the government, and creating institutions whose authority does not depend on proximity to the prime minister.

    Read more

    The Orban-Netanyahu mutual support nexus

    Older Hungarians understandably speak about restoration: rebuilding institutions, restoring judicial independence, returning to democratic normality.

    But “return” means something different when you are 25. You cannot return to a political world you never inhabited. For younger Hungarians, democracy cannot merely be recovered; it has to become real for the first time.

    That distinction matters beyond Hungary. Opponents of personalised populism often offer restoration as their programme.

    Yet generations raised amid democratic erosion may have little memory of the normality they are being asked to recover. Democratic politics has to show that dispersed power need not mean ineffective government, that disagreement need not threaten the state, and that losing an election need not mean losing the country.

    Success should also mean making politics less consuming. Most democratic life is not election night but local meetings, newspapers and arguments about schools, budgets and public space.

    A healthy political order allows citizens to pay less attention to the leader because fewer things depend on what that leader wants. Personalised rule teaches the opposite lesson. Even resistance can become dependence.

    This is where Hungary’s experience returns me to my conversation about Israel.

    Israelis are due to vote on 27 October in an election in which Netanyahu once again occupies much of the political landscape.

    Read more

    No candidate in Israeli election backs a Palestinian state. The EU’s answer is more ‘reforms’, not pressure

    Whatever voters decide, Hungary suggests a question that will remain whenever his long political era eventually ends: can political life be reorganised around institutions and competing interests rather than around the presence, or absence, of one man?

    Removing a dominant political figure does not remove the habits formed around him. Supporters have to imagine their politics without the leader they regarded as indispensable, while opponents have to decide what they stand for when opposition to him is no longer enough to bind them together.

    Hungary’s experience suggests that this is where democratic renewal really begins – not with replacing one dominant figure with another, but with building institutions and political movements that no longer require one.

    My friend’s tears were for the time she felt had been taken from her. Hungary’s younger generation, now free of Orbán, cannot mourn in quite the same way, because many have no memory of political adulthood against which to measure what was lost.

    Their challenge, now, is not to recover an old normal but to create something they have never experienced: a public life in which politics belongs to citizens without consuming them, and in which no leader becomes so indispensable that an entire country must organise itself around him.

    ]]>         EU vows to stop buying Arctic oil and gas, but drops ban from its new strategy https://euobserver.com/243804/eu-vows-to-stop-buying-arctic-oil-and-gas-but-drops-ban-from-its-new-strategy/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 14:40:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243804 EU officials vowed an end to Arctic oil and gas buying, as the European Commission presented its new Arctic strategy. But while the document commits to keeping Arctic oil and gas “in the ground,” it drops the call for an international ban.]]> The EU “will not drill and will not buy” Arctic oil and gas, EU officials said on Tuesday (20 October), as the European Commission presented its new Arctic strategy.

    Of the €800bn announced under ReArm Europe in March 2025, €650bn is not common money. It is an estimate of the extra room governments get under the national escape clause to spend up to 1.5 percent of GDP more on defence for four years.

    Each country still pays for that spending itself.

    The room is also temporary: EU Commission simulations suggest that maintaining higher defence spending after 2028 could require additional annual fiscal adjustment of 0.25 to 0.4 percentage points of GDP from 2029.

    The other €150bn is SAFE, and it is loans, not grants.

    The EU borrows and lends the money on, and each country repays its share. Grants are small: €1.5bn from the European Defence Industry Programme for 2025-2027, plus the European Defence Fund for joint research.

    Not every country has used these tools, as Table 1 shows. The Netherlands and Sweden have used neither. Like Germany, which has taken only the clause, they can borrow at least as cheaply as the EU, so SAFE gets them nothing.

    France has taken SAFE but not the clause, to protect the credibility of its budget plans.

    Source: Council of the EU, European Commission. Data as of 17 October 2026. * Hungary: allocated €16.2bn, now requesting €5.4bn; still pending. ** Italy: the Commission backed its request on 8 October 2026; the Council has yet to decide.

    Where SAFE does matter is on the eastern flank. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia can borrow the equivalent of five to eight percent of their GDP, and Poland almost five percent.

    That leaves private money.

    In Tirana, students joined wider demonstrations over education costs and corruption allegations.

    These are not parts of a single movement, and the protests do not have one common cause. But they bring into focus a shared challenge: whether young people can see a credible route from education to decent work, and from financial dependence to a life of their own. 

    France: school conditions shape the starting line

    Since September, French students have demonstrated over teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and deteriorating school buildings. Their demands concern more than the day-to-day running of schools. They also raise a question about equal opportunity: can public education give every student the tools to move forward, regardless of where they live or what their family can afford?

    The wider figures help explain why that question matters.

    In 2025, 25.5 percent of people aged 15–29 in France were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 24.2 percent across the EU, according to Eurostat.

    In August 2026, unemployment among under-25s stood at 20.6 percent, against 8.2 percent for the population as a whole. The corresponding EU rates were 15.4 percent and 6.1 percent.

    Read more

    The forgotten protests: empty shelves and blocked roads in southern Italy, ignored by the media, reveal neglect by Meloni and EU

    These figures do not show that school shortages cause youth unemployment. They do show how difficult the step from education into work remains for many young people and why well-resourced schools matter most in areas with the fewest opportunities.

    Housing can make that transition harder still. In Paris, one-in-two private tenants under 30 spends more than 51 percent of their income on rent. A Eurostat indicator also shows that 70 percent of 20–24-year-olds and 25 percent of 25–29-year-olds either live with their parents or are financially connected to their household. 

    France scored 66 out of 100 and ranked 27th of 182 countries in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index. The index measures perceptions of public-sector corruption, not the number of proven incidents. It does not explain the school protests, but it underlines why transparency and accountability matter when public services and resources are at stake.

    Spain: when housing delays independence

    Abascal’s eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for decades prompted demonstrations in several Spanish cities and renewed calls for stronger tenant protections. Her case was not a youth protest, but it put a human face on a housing crisis that also shapes whether younger people can leave home and build an independent life.

    In 2025, 67.1 percent of Spaniards aged 18–34 lived with at least one parent, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute.

    Among those living with a parent, 28.3 percent said they could not afford to rent. The average age at which young people left home was 30.2, compared with 26.3 across the EU, according to Eurostat.

    Housing pressure does not operate in isolation. In 2025, 27.6 percent of Spaniards aged 15–29 were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, above the EU rate of 24.2%.

    In August 2026, unemployment among under-25s was 22.7 percent, more than twice the overall rate of 10 percent. When joblessness is so much higher among the young and rent is beyond the reach of many, delayed independence cannot be reduced to personal preference.

    Spain scored 55/100 in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 49th of 182 countries. That score does not establish a link between corruption and housing protests. But when people are asking for effective action on housing, transparency over how decisions are made — and accountability for whether they work — are part of the debate.

    Albania: growth is not enough if young people see no path forward

    In October, students in Tirana protested over education costs and corruption allegations, joining a broader anti-government movement. Their participation brought education and young people’s prospects into a wider debate about living costs, employment and trust in public institutions.

    Albania’s official figures show that 19 percent of the population was at risk of relative poverty in 2025, while 31.2 percent experienced severe material and social deprivation, according to INSTAT. The two measures describe different aspects of hardship: one compares household income with the national poverty threshold; the other captures enforced inability to afford basic goods and activities.

    Young people also face a difficult entry into the labour market. The World Bank’s ILO-modelled estimates put overall unemployment at 10.9 percent in 2025, rising to 25.6 percent among 15–24-year-olds. The estimated average age of leaving the parental household seemed to be 30.9, compared with 26.3 in the EU, according to Eurostat’s dataset. Together, however, these indicators describe the hurdles between education, employment and independence.

    Albania scored 39/100 and ranked 91st of 182 countries in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index. The measure is not a count of actual cases, but corruption allegations are part of the protests themselves. That makes transparency, accountability and public trust more than abstract principles: they shape whether people believe institutions respond fairly to their concerns.

    Behind the statistics

    Behind the statistics are millions of young people struggling to turn their ambitions into reality. The obstacles reinforce one another: under-resourced schools can narrow choices, unemployment can delay financial independence, and high housing costs can prolong dependence on family.

    Across the EU, house prices rose by 55.4 percent and rents by 26.7 percent between 2010 and 2024, often outpacing income growth, according to Eurofound.

    That is why the response cannot be confined to one policy area. It means properly staffed and maintained schools, routes from education into decent work, more affordable and social housing, targeted help with rent, and stronger protections for tenants.

    Young people should also have a meaningful say in policies that shape their education, employment and housing.

    A strong welfare state and effective social protection can help ensure that a young person’s prospects are not determined solely by family income or place of birth. If a low-income family cannot support a young person’s move towards independence, financial dependence can pass from one generation to the next. Tackling that cycle is part of building social justice and societies in which young people can plan a future with greater confidence.

    The future will show whether today’s protests lead to lasting policies. The test will be whether young people can study, find decent work and afford a home without their prospects being set by the circumstances into which they were born.

]]> Après une escale à La Réunion l’année dernière, le Fundtruck a de nouveau posé ses valises dans l’océan Indien, en associant cette fois La Réunion et Mayotte au sein d’une même étape. Le 24 septembre, Maddyness a ainsi organisé une étape hybride depuis le siège de la BRED à Saint-Denis, permettant aux entrepreneuses et entrepreneurs des deux territoires de présenter leur projet dans les mêmes conditions que les candidats de l’Hexagone.

Une étape entre La Réunion et Mayotte

Huit startups réunionnaises et mahoraises étaient en lice pour décrocher leur place en finale. Comme à chaque étape du Fundtruck, les entrepreneurs disposaient de trois minutes pour pitcher leur projet, avant cinq minutes de questions face à un jury composé d’investisseurs et d’acteurs de l’écosystème.

Pour cette édition particulière, 16 membres du jury se sont mobilisés, sur place à La Réunion ou à distance, afin d’écouter et de challenger les différents projets. 

À l’issue des délibérations, c’est CapstonAI qui s’est imposée auprès du jury. Fondée par Greg Hanffou, la startup accompagne les entreprises pour améliorer leur visibilité dans les réponses générées par les principaux outils d’intelligence artificielle, comme ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude et Perplexity.

Faire rayonner les écosystèmes ultramarins

Cette étape a permis de mettre une nouvelle fois en lumière le dynamisme entrepreneurial de territoires encore éloignés des grands hubs de l’innovation métropolitains. 

L’étape 2026 a pu aussi compter sur le soutien de la BRED Banque Populaire, partenaire de cette escale, ainsi que de La French Tech La Réunion, Bpifrance, IVECO, Electra, CF Advisory et CF - Compagnie Fiduciaire, avec Manuel Biota.

CapstonAI rejoint désormais les autres lauréats de la saison et se prépare à représenter La Réunion et Mayotte lors de la Grande Finale du Fundtruck 2026. Celle-ci aura lieu le 26 novembre au siège de LCL.. La tournée, elle, se poursuit avec des nouvelles étapes en Île-de-France, en Belgique, puis à Bordeaux.

      <description><p>Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/21/french-borrowing-costs-failure-to-pass-budget-govenment-bonds-violent-street-protests</link>
      <description><p>Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests</p><p></p><p>France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.</p><p>With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/21/french-borrowing-costs-failure-to-pass-budget-govenment-bonds-violent-street-protests">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Billionaire, on SpaceX earnings call, says ‘special committees’ exploring idea but no agreement reached yet</p><p>As SpaceX released its second-ever public earnings report on Tuesday, Elon Musk declared his support for combining the aerospace and AI company with his electric vehicle company, Tesla.       <title>Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/20/ai-actors-val-kilmer-as-deep-as-the-grave-tilly-norwood</link>
      <description><p>As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner</p><p>‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.</p><p>Not just yet, judging by the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G0L8wTLaS8U">extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year</a>: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/20/ai-actors-val-kilmer-as-deep-as-the-grave-tilly-norwood">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 21 Oct 2026 15:58:10 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Pretax profits at yoghurt maker Glenilen Farm rise 56% to €1.6m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/pretax-profits-at-yoghurt-maker-glenilen-farm-rise-56-to-16m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/pretax-profits-at-yoghurt-maker-glenilen-farm-rise-56-to-16m/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 15:53:16 +0000Pretax profits at yoghurt-maker Glenilen Farm last year increased by 56 per cent to €1.65 million on the back of record revenues.

Accounts filed by the family run Glenilen Farm Ltd, based in west Cork, show that profits rose as sales increased by 25 per cent to a record €15.8 million in 2025.

The business started in 1997 with Alan Kingston on the farm and Valerie Kingston in the kitchen, producing and selling products at local markets in Cork.

At the end of December last, accumulated profits had climbed to €4.62 million. In 2025 numbers employed at the firm increased from 73 to 84.

The firm’s post-tax profits of €1.45 million for 2025 follow post tax profits of €930,826 in 2024.

Cash funds last year increased from €202,442 to €347,071.

Net assets at the company last year rose from €3.43 million to €4.88 million.

Co-founder Alan Kingston said on Wednesday that growth in 2025 “was driven by strong consumer demand across Glenilen Farm’s core product ranges, continued innovation and expanding domestic and export sales”.

The firm has also expanded its presence in export markets including the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Macau and Singapore with the total export market accounting for 9 per cent of turnover in 2025.

Kingston said “while we’re very pleased with our 2025 results, and the continued strong performance of the business in 2026, it has not been without its challenges as rising input costs are having an impact on every business”.

He said “our focus remains firmly on the opportunity ahead. More than half of the yoghurt consumed in Ireland is still imported, which means there remains significant potential for Irish producers like Glenilen Farm to win a greater share of the domestic market.”

“As consumers become more conscious about where their food comes from, we believe there is a real opportunity for Irish-made dairy products to continue gaining ground,” Kingston said.

On the rise in profits last year, Kingston said that the increase in profitability in 2025 was the result of a long-term growth strategy rather than short-term market conditions or cost-cutting measures.

“Over recent years, Glenilen Farm has reinvested profits back into the business, with significant investment in factory expansion, automation, innovation and operational efficiencies,” he said.

The profits last year take account of net non-cash depreciation costs of €553,514.

Directors’ pay, including pension payments, last year increased from €166,229 to €180,296.

]]><![CDATA[Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/21/revoluts-outage-was-a-warning-to-us-all/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/21/revoluts-outage-was-a-warning-to-us-all/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 15:02:56 +0000Tuesday was a tough day to be dependent on Revolut. Customers trying to make card payments as normal were refused. Cash withdrawals were also affected, leaving some people with no access at all to their money. If they were lucky enough to be able to log into the app, the in-app support was unresponsive, and Revolut does not routinely offer phone support to its customers.

It was, in short, a bit of a disaster for the digital bank. Revolut was quick to reassure people that their money and data were safe, but that didn’t help those who were stranded without a way to pay for travel or buy food.

It would be easy to shrug and say that people should always have a backup. A second bank card with a different financial institution; perhaps some emergency cash just in case (did none of us read the Government’s emergency booklet?) to get us through.

There but for the grace of the tech gods go all of us. The problem wasn’t down to Revolut’s systems, or a cyberattack, but a failure at Google Cloud. The company has made a concerted push into the financial services market as it vies for business with rivals Microsoft and AWS.

It could have been any bank ; this time, it just happened to be Revolut, a relative newcomer to the banking world that is still treated dismissively by some. This is despite the fact that more than 3 million people in Ireland use the digital bank’s services. It has lured away a good number of those users from Ireland’s traditional banks, and forced them into providing better digital services to customers.

And it wasn’t just Revolut that was affected. Although AIB and Bank of Ireland reported no problems with their services, in the UK, Lloyds and HSBC also suffered the effects of the outage. The UK’s courts video system was taken down too.

Why is motor insurance so expensive in Ireland?

The issue that Revolut’s outage raised is not that we should turn away from digital banks; it is the fact that we are overly dependent on a small number of tech systems in every facet of our daily lives. Take out one and the cascade effect is terrifying to behold.

These incidents are relatively rare, but they happen. Ironically, it was a year to the day that a big problem with AWS’s services caused apps such as Fortnite and Snapchat to go dark. That was followed only days later by a Microsoft Azure issue, an “inadvertent configuration change” that not only knocked Microsoft’s own services offline, but also took down airlines, Heathrow airport, even An Post.

They are, in a way, a victim of their own success. If Google, Microsoft, and AWS were not supporting as many of the day-to-day services we use, we wouldn’t notice if the service had a minor blip. But they do, and consequently, when things go wrong, the impact is widespread.

It is not just the infrastructure that underpins these services that is out of our hands. After US president Donald Trump imposed sanctions on a French judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Nicolas Guillou, he found that his access to many of the services we take for granted has been effectively blocked. Travel bookings made through Expedia have been cancelled. His bank account has been restricted, and booking flights or other transport is almost impossible for him.

Imagine if you could not access your email or cloud storage services. How many mobile numbers have you committed to memory, because you know they are stored safely on your phone? How much of your life would be affected if you could no longer use your bank card?

The sanctions, which were imposed on a number of ICC judges and block US entities and their overseas subsidiaries from providing services to him, came following investigations into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan and Palestine and the issuing of arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

Imagine if you could not access your email or cloud storage services. How many mobile numbers have you committed to memory, because you know they are stored safely on your phone? How much of your life would be affected if you could no longer use your bank card?

More recently, the reported slowdown of Starlink’s satellite communications system in Ukraine affected the country’s ability to defend itself. Ukraine relies on the system to help intercept Russian missile and drone attacks; speed limits that were imposed last week made that a more difficult task.

According to the Wall Street Journal, that slowdown came at the order of billionaire Elon Musk. Musk appeared to point the finger at the White House, but the US has denied involvement.

Regardless of who was responsible, the end result was the same: a powerful billionaire somewhere put a thumb on the scale and ordinary people suffered the consequences.

These incidents all highlight our precarious position in Europe. Whether it is a concentration of business in a small number of tech firms or the shifting geopolitical landscape, Europe needs to get some sort of control over things.

Proposals published by the European Commission in June set a number of targets to help achieve this, from increasing data centre capacity to supporting chip production. Bureaucracy moves slowly, though, and EU bureaucracy is a particular behemoth. The targets set are still a good way off, and Europe is starting from behind.

The alternative, though, is throwing up our hands and giving up. To adapt a phrase, the best time to start developing tech sovereignty was yesterday; the second best time is now.

Europe needs alternatives, and it needs them fast.

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Aviation firm co-founder ousted during sick leave wins €41,000 for unfair dismissal at WRC]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/aviation-firm-founder-ousted-during-sick-leave-wins-41000-for-unfair-dismissal-at-wrc/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/aviation-firm-founder-ousted-during-sick-leave-wins-41000-for-unfair-dismissal-at-wrc/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 18:01:19 +0000

An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.

Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.

Having been paid an “eight-figure” sum for his shareholding, Burke moved to Malta for tax reasons, and stepped down as managing director to a new post as director of special projects, the company’s lawyers submitted.

His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.

A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.

The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.

It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.

Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.

His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.

It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.

The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.

Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.

Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.

In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.

In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.

After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.

There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.

Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.

The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.

Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.

She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.

However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.

Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.

This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.

Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley.

*This article was amended on 21st of October to make clear that Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, Gerry Burke, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley and that Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, Magellan Aviation, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors.

]]><![CDATA[Avoca’s Kilmacanogue and Rathcoole stores hit the market with €29m price tag]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/10/21/avocas-kilmacanogue-and-rathcoole-stores-hit-the-market-with-29m-price-tag/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/10/21/avocas-kilmacanogue-and-rathcoole-stores-hit-the-market-with-29m-price-tag/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:55:00 +0000Having paid about €22 million to acquire two of Avoca’s flagship premises from the retailer’s US-headquartered owner, Aramark, in 2017, Irish retail property investor Signature Capital is now looking to dispose of the properties.

The sale of Avoca’s outlets at Kilmacanogue in Co Wicklow and Rathcoole in Co Dublin is expected to provide Signature’s private clients with a healthy return on their original investment. The two properties are being offered to the market by joint agents JLL and TWM, fully let to Avoca until 2047, with Aramark (US) as guarantor, at a guide price of €29 million.

Avoca Kilmacanogue is arguably the retailer’s best-known outlet apart from the company’s original mill in Avoca village. Located just off the N11, the store, which first opened for business under Avoca’s former owners, Donald Pratt and his wife Hilary in 1979, has long proved to be a draw for the affluent and densely populated south Dublin and Wicklow catchment area. It is also hugely popular with tourists and day-trippers travelling to the nearby attractions of Glendalough and Avondale Forest Park.

Avoca Kilmacanogue comprises a distinctive lifestyle and retail premises extending to 2,570sq m (27,663sq ft) on a landscaped site of 6.39 hectares (15.79 acres). Developed over a number of phases, the accommodation includes a large retail offering consisting of convenience, food, homewares and fashion, together with the Sugar Tree Cafe, Fern House Restaurant, a bakery, garden centre, ancillary accommodation and extensive cold-storage facilities.

The site may have longer term potential for residential development, subject to planning permission, according to the selling agents.

Avoca’s Rathcoole outlet is located just off the N7 Naas Road, close to junction 4 of the M7/M50 interchange, and about 16km southwest of Dublin city centre.

Developed in 2007, the property comprises a three-storey building of 3,964sq m (42,668sq ft) on a site of 1.6 hectares (3.95 acres) with frontage to both the N7 Naas Road and Fitzmaurice Road.

The ground floor consists of extensive retail and ancillary space, while the first floor is home to the Egg Cafe and Birdcage Cafe, together with kitchen facilities and balcony seating areas. The second floor comprises modern office accommodation accessed via a dedicated entrance and passenger lift, with a mix of occupiers including Avoca.

Both the Kilmacanogue and Rathcoole properties are let on long-term leases with 21 years left until expiry. The tenant is currently paying total annual rent of €1,680,000. Rent reviews occur every five years and are linked to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), subject to a 3.5 per cent annual cap and -0.5 per cent annual collar, compounded annually.

The rent is guaranteed by Avoca’s parent company Aramark (US). Aramark acquired the Avoca business from the Pratt family in a €66.7 million* deal in 2015.

The next CPI rental uplift is due in September 2027, with the rent payable increasing to €2 million at that time. The vendor is providing a rental underwrite to ensure that the incoming owner will secure a yield of 6.2 per cent based on the asking price of €29 million.

Sean O’Neill of TWM says: “Opportunities of this calibre rarely come to the market, combining the security of such a recognisable tenant with the benefit of long-term secure income. This portfolio offers investors an exceptional opportunity to secure stable and predictable cash flows, making it particularly attractive to those seeking wealth preservation, inflation protection and long-duration income in a premier retail and hospitality asset.”

Max Reilly of JLL adds: “This is an exceptional asset with long-term, inflation-proof income backed by an outstanding guarantor.”

*This article was amended to include the correct price paid by Aramark for the Avoca business. Reports published in 2015 and 2016 suggested the deal carried a lower value of between €51 and €60 million

]]>Peter Moloney<![CDATA[Legal technology start-up Estatemin raises €1m in pre-seed funding]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/legal-technology-start-up-estatemin-raises-1m-in-pre-seed-funding/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/legal-technology-start-up-estatemin-raises-1m-in-pre-seed-funding/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 12:55:32 +0000Irish-founded legal technology start-up Estatemin has raised €1 million in a pre-seed round to help support its growth in the US.

The company, which was founded by Isabella Hughes, Oisín Dolphin and John Noonan, is building a platform powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and focused on trust and estate law firms in the US, helping them to reduce their administrative workload.

The platform can digitise client intake, organise estate information, extract data from documents and support form preparation, helping law firms to save between five and seven hours on an estate-planning matter, with up to 10 hours on estate administrations.

The pre-seed funding round saw participation from NDRC, First Port Syndicate and angel investors Mike Hanrahan, Moira McKenna and Conor Stanley, among other Irish angels.

Enterprise Ireland has also backed the company through its High Potential Startup programme. Now headquartered in New York, Estatemin will use the money to accelerate customer acquisition in the US, expand its engineering and product teams, and support its go-to-market function.

Its engineering operation will remain in Ireland and the UK. The company employs eight people, with one based in the US. However, the priorities for hiring have shifted, Hughes said.

“AI has got so good that you can do so much with so little these days,” she said. “We need more people on the go-to-market front, that’s an area we could hire tomorrow. By the end of next year we are probably looking at a team of around 15 people.”

The company was born from a meeting between Hughes, who is a law graduate, and Dolphin through an NDRC founder weekend at Dogpatch Labs in 2024. Dolphin had been through the probate process, which is paper-heavy, following the death of his father.

Hughes said her experience of working in the industry matched Dolphin’s. That posed a simple question: why are highly trained legal professionals spending so much time retyping information?

The duo founded the company as Simple Probate, with Noonan subsequently coming on board as the third cofounder, bringing his experience of working with legal technology company Clio to the start-up.

Initially focused on Irish law firms, the company changed tack and focused on the US market, which was faster to adopt the platform.

Estatemin partnered with Clio and now supports law firms across all 50 US states. It has grown revenue 20 per cent month on month, with companies using the platform managing more than $770 million (€685 million) in estate value.

“We are growing quickly right now,” Hughes said. “We are always looking ahead and getting ready for that next round.”

]]><![CDATA[Moving from America to Ireland for work? Here’s what you need to know]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/21/thinking-of-moving-from-the-us-to-ireland-for-work-heres-what-you-need-to-know/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/21/thinking-of-moving-from-the-us-to-ireland-for-work-heres-what-you-need-to-know/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000The number of US citizens moving to Ireland has more than doubled in recent years, while Irish recruiters have seen “growing interest” from professionals based overseas.

An estimated 10,000 people moved to Ireland from the US in the 12 months leading up to April this year, up from 4,900 in the same period two years prior, according to data from the Central Statistics Office.

More than half (53 per cent) of the overall number of immigrants in that period were of working age, between 25 and 44, while just 3 per cent were aged 65 or older.

Although the majority of job applications continue to come from those already based in Ireland or elsewhere in Europe, Matrix Recruitment has seen a “growing interest” from professionals based overseas, such as in the US.

But what should US citizens know before making the move to the Republic for work?

Meet the Americans moving to Ireland for a better life

Securing a job offer is the first step, as employers often assess visa requirements early in the hiring process, according to Breda Dooley, head of recruitment at Matrix.

Where permits are required, timelines and recruitment decisions can be impacted, she says.

“Our advice to US professionals considering a move is to research permit eligibility, understand salary thresholds and ensure their qualifications and experience align with occupations currently in demand,” she says.

Dooley adds that experience gained within US markets can often be viewed “positively” by employers based in Ireland.

“That said, employers generally favour candidates who either already have the right to work in Ireland or whose skills clearly justify sponsorship through an employment permit process,” she says.

The two most common routes available to US citizens hoping to move to and work in Ireland are the critical skills employment permit and the general employment permit.

Dooley says the critical skills permit, which targets highly skilled workers, is an “important mechanism” to attract talent into areas where demand exceeds the available domestic workforce.

Such job opportunities are most commonly found in software development, cybersecurity and data analytics, engineering, pharmaceutical and life sciences sectors, as well as finance and certain healthcare professions.

The Department of Enterprise maintains a full list of critical skills occupations while such roles require a minimum salary of €40,904.

Once a worker has completed 21 months on a critical skills permit, they can apply for Stamp 4 permission to work in Ireland without an employment permit.

‘I’m an American, can I live in Ireland for six months of the year?’

General employment permits, on the other hand, are open to all occupations, with the exception of those listed as ineligible by the department.

However, this route is less straight forward as employers are required to undertake a labour needs test first. If no suitable candidate applies for the role, the employer can then apply for a general employment permit.

The role must have a minimum salary of €36,605, though the salary for meat processors, horticultural workers, healthcare assistants and home carers must be at least €32,691.

Workers on general employment permits must complete 57 months before they are eligible to apply for Stamp 4 permission.

Moira Grassick, chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland, cautions that an employment permit does not automatically grant someone the right to enter or live in Ireland.

“Anyone moving to Ireland from outside the EU should also ensure that they have registered with the immigration service and obtained the appropriate immigration permission for a long-term stay,” she says.

Once an employment permit is secured and after moving, US citizens must obtain an Irish residence permit at a cost of €300 for the initial application and for subsequent renewals.

Those who successfully secure employment must also obtain a PPS number in order to get paid and register with Revenue, she says, adding they should also familiarise themselves with their rights and obligations as an employee in Ireland.
