]]><![CDATA[Netflix sales growth to slow for fourth quarter ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/netflix-sales-growth-to-slow-for-fourth-quarter/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/netflix-sales-growth-to-slow-for-fourth-quarter/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 06:31:29 +0000Netflix reported its slowest sales jump in three years and forecast a fourth consecutive quarter of slowing growth, a projection that amplifies concerns about the world’s leading online TV network.

Netflix delivered sales of $12.9 billion (€11.5 billion) in the third quarter, in line with Wall Street’s expectations, and forecast sales of $13.4 billion in the year’s final three months, falling short of what analysts have predicted. The pace of growth has fallen from 17.6 per cent in the final quarter of last year to a projection of 11.5 per cent for this year’s fourth quarter.

The company blamed its sales shortfall on the advertising business, which is on pace to deliver $300 million less than the company expected.

Shares fell as much as 7 per cent in trading after the results were announced.

“I know we can do better,” Netflix co-chief executive Greg Peters said on a call with analysts Tuesday. “That better is our upside.”

Over the past week, Peters and co-CEO Ted Sarandos have overhauled the company’s leadership to address what they see as a decline in programming quality. Netflix fired chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin just days after announcing cuts of 6 per cent of the staff, or about 1,000 people. The last time Netflix made such substantial reductions was in 2022, when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years.

The company’s operating margin forecast for the fourth quarter of 26 per cent is impacted by costs associated with the job cuts. Earnings of 87 cents per share in the third quarter exceeded analysts’ projections for 82 cents.

Sarandos and Peters are walking a tightrope, seeking to assure investors that the company has a bright future while acknowledging things aren’t going as well as everyone would like. Netflix remains a clear leader in streaming. It has more than 325 million subscribers, which the company says equates to almost 1 billion viewers. It accounts for more viewing than any other Hollywood streaming service.

But Hollywood studios don’t overhaul their programming teams when everything is hunky dory. Netflix has gone months without a large, culture-shaping hit in film or TV and has struggled to lure viewers to both new shows and new seasons of older shows. Netflix’s haul of Emmy Awards fell to a 10-year low in 2026.

Sarandos and Peters brought in Peter Rice, a veteran film and TV executive who previously served as chairman of general entertainment at Walt Disney Co, and before that as president of 21st century Fox, to replace Bajaria.

“We see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the US,” Sarandos said, touting Rice’s experience in all aspects of entertainment. Rice has worked in film and TV as both an executive and a producer. He also has deep relationships with top filmmakers.

“We want Netflix to always be the place people want to do the best work of their life,” Sarandos said.

Long a Wall Street darling, Netflix has faced growing scepticism ever since it made a play to buy the streaming and studios businesses of Warner Bros Discovery.

After losing out in its bid, Netflix has struggled to convince investors it has a viable growth strategy. The stock is down about 25 per cent this year and more than 40 per cent from a year ago.

Investors and analysts have pestered Netflix’s leadership about stagnant engagement. Netflix’s share of US TV viewership sits at 7.8 per cent, according to ratings tracker Nielsen, far behind YouTube, which captures about 14 per cent. And Netflix viewers watched only 2 per cent more programming in the first half of the year than a year earlier.

As Netflix has grown from a small US streaming service into a global behemoth, it has evolved from a producer of “prestige TV” shows like House of Cards and The Crown to a broader entertainment platform, competing with everything from sports channels to YouTube influencers.

Bajaria led the division that released hits like Squid Game and Wednesday, and helped shepherd Netflix’s live programming era with sports and an expanded unscripted portfolio.

But Bajaria’s hot touch cooled over the last year, and many began to question the quality of Netflix’s programming.

“Investors will need, in short order, some indications toward confidence in the growth trajectory that this powerful, global platform should be able to provide,” David Joyce, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said in a note before the results were released.

Netflix is seeking to increase the amount of time its users spend on the service by expanding into live sports, podcasts and video games while also integrating film and TV programming from third parties like TF1 in France. Peters said the company is open to integrating programming from other companies and will also look to sell other streaming services within Netflix. -Bloomberg

]]>Jim Vondruska<![CDATA[Are women in your workplace earning less? A new Government website lifts the lid]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/21/are-women-in-your-workplace-earning-less-a-new-government-website-lifts-the-lid/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/21/are-women-in-your-workplace-earning-less-a-new-government-website-lifts-the-lid/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Do women in your workplace have the same average earnings as men? A new Government website will make it easier for you to find out.

Ireland’s national gender pay gap stands at 8.3 per cent, according to figures quoted by the Department of Equality this year. That’s the average difference in pay between all men and all women in the workforce. If you’re a woman working in an organisation on the wrong side of the gap, it pays to know about it.

New data published from next month aims to lift the lid on gaps in pay and equip you to find out how your workplace measures up.

New portal

By the end of November, all employers with more than 50 employees must publish data about their gender pay gap to a new public gender pay gap portal.

The gender pay gap is the average difference in pay between all men and all women in an organisation. If you are a woman working in an organisation where there is a big gap, it doesn’t bode well for your finances.

The pay portal has been open for voluntary reporting since last year and viewable to the public since June, but publication by employers is about to become mandatory.

The Employment Equality Bill 2026 will be enacted in the coming weeks, with individual company gender pay gap figures for 2026 available to view by the end of November, Minister for Equality Norma Foley told the Dáil last week.

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) put Ireland’s national gender pay gap at 9.6 per cent in 2022. Mean hourly earnings for men were €27.73 and €25.06 for women, a gap of €2.67.

As age increases, the gender pay gap grows. The biggest gap was in the 50-59 age group at 16.7 per cent, with men earning €33.03 and women earning €27.51.

Sectors such as construction, aviation and finance tend to show wider gaps due to male-dominated senior roles, while education and healthcare often show the opposite trend.

In many cases, it’s less about pay rates and more about representation at senior levels, says UCD’s Professional Academy.

It’s important to note the gender pay gap is not a test of whether men and women in an organisation are paid equally for the same work – that’s already required by law. Rather, it highlights imbalances that influence how opportunities are distributed, according to the academy.

If your organisation has a big gender pay gap, there may be some telltale signs.

There are probably fewer women in senior or higher-paid roles; there is an over-representation of women in lower-paid or part-time roles in a company; maybe there is unconscious bias or barriers to the progression of women; there is a culture where availing of hybrid working is frowned on; or maybe there is a culture where the men who work there never take leave for caring responsibilities.

Female participation in Irish workforce jumps 90% since 2000

Some or all of these characteristics can contribute to a workplace where pay between genders is out of whack.

If you work in or are interviewing for a role in an organisation with a big pay gap, the impact can ripple far beyond your pay cheque.

Lower average pay than male colleagues in an organisation can mean women there get a smaller percentage pay rise than male colleagues, receive a less generous pay-linked bonus, are unable to borrow as much their male colleagues can to buy a house, and end up with smaller pensions in retirement.

If you are already in a job or scouting for a new one, the new pay gap portal will make it easier to look under the bonnet and see the reality of the hiring, pay, promotion practices and culture there.

Scores on the doors

Gender pay gap reporting requires employers to choose a snapshot day in June this year, and use pay information for the previous 12 months for their pay gap calculations. Employers then have five months to publish their report, by the end of November.

Some 1,000 employers have now created accounts on the portal in preparation for publishing their reports by the end of next month, the Department of Equality says.

Some firms have been proactive, voluntarily publishing their 2025 pay gap data to the portal. You’ll find 410 such reports already published.

Searching the portal by company name and looking for the mean, or average gender pay gap, is a useful metric for employees, says Michelle McDonagh, chief client officer at human resource management consultancy Adare.

If you see a large gender pay gap percentage, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the organisation is paying women unfairly, says McDonagh.

“Gender pay gap measures the pay of all men and compares it against all women. There is no allowance for the type of role, length of service, level of seniority or expertise,” she says.

“It’s a blunt instrument in that regard.”

The gender pay gap figure, however, is a useful indicator of hiring and promotion practices, policies and culture in a company.

Being a working mother is a horror show at times. The stress can be crippling

A zero per cent pay gap is the ideal. That would mean men and women’s pay is perfectly balanced.

A positive gender pay gap, of five per cent for example, means women earn five per cent less on average than men. A negative, or minus gap, means men earn less than women on average.

“Most organisations will have a positive figure because in most organisations, women will earn less than men on average,” says McDonagh.

Comparing companies by sector can provide an interesting perspective.

Take the telecommunications, computer programming and consulting sector in the data, for example. This is one of the most highly remunerated sectors in the country. Consultancy firm Deloitte has been proactive in publishing its data and reports a 5.2 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in favour of men.

Another useful search in the portal is “distribution of gender by pay quartile”. This requires bosses to segment their workforce by pay band and tell you the balance of men and women in each of four different bands. Looking at Deloitte, there were 10 per cent more women than men in the lower middle pay band in 2025, but 4 per cent more men than women in the very top pay band.

“One of the trends we tend to see in companies is if there are a lot of females coming into lower-paid roles and for whatever reason they are not progressing through the ranks,” says McDonagh.

“Then you see a lot of males in the higher-paid roles and women’s representation drops away as they move through those different pay quartiles.”

What top CEO pay and gender pay gap reporting tell us about Irish business

Companies are required to publish a statement about what is causing their pay gap and what they are going to do about it.

Deloitte’s statement says the company has met its target of 35 per cent female partners by 2025.

“We aim to increase this to 40 per cent by 2027, with a 50 per cent longer-term goal,” according to the firm.

Data for PwC shows a 1.6 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in the mean hourly pay of female and male employees.

Women and men are 50:50 in the lowest pay quartile, but there are 10 per cent more women than men in the topmost pay quartile.

‘Women make up at least half of our population. This, in turn, has had a significant influence on the outcome of our gender pay gap analysis,” says PwC.

KPMG, Ernst & Young (EY) or Accenture have not published data on the portal for 2025. They will be required to publish their 2026 data by the end of November.

They were required to publish 2025 pay gap data on their own websites, however.

KPMG reports an average gender pay gap of 11.1 per cent for 2025 – the organisation comprises 51 per cent women and 49 per cent men. There are more women than men in all three lower pay quartiles, but 11 per cent more men at the top pay quartile.

There is a 23.2 per cent average bonus gap between men and women at the consulting firm, its report says.

At partner level, women represent 24 per cent of partners. The pay gap between female and male partners is 5.6 per cent.

Pay transparency rules could cause conflict in workplaces, say HR and law experts

The mean pay gap at Accenture for 2025 is 9.2 per cent. The number of women and men are almost equal in all pay quartiles – except at the top one where there are 10 per cent more men in the highest pay grade.

The mean pay gap at EY for 2025 is 6.5 per cent. Some 71 per cent of partners are male.

Meta Platforms Ireland, which employs 95 per cent of Meta’s staff here, has a 2025 gender pay gap of 26.5 per cent, and an average bonus pay gap of 37 per cent.

The company employs an almost equal number of men and women. The number of women at Meta is greatest in its lowest pay quartile, where there are 62 per cent women, and the number of women is fewest in the highest pay quartile, where there are 63 per cent men.

Women are better represented in non-tech roles in the company, Meta says. Tech roles, like software engineers, are typically paid more in the market, and this has a disproportionate impact on pay gaps, it says.

The bonus gap is higher than the hourly pay gap, which is primarily driven by higher tech equity, it says.

Hooke & MacDonald is the only large real estate firm to have voluntarily published its gender pay gap data to the Government portal for 2025. It reports a 13 per cent gender pay gap in the mean hourly pay of female employees and of male employees.

“We are clear that our pay gap arises as a result of a greater proportion of males in senior positions in specific areas of the business and on higher pay points within those grades – due to longer service in those roles. This significantly contributes to the pay gap,” the company says.

Government organisations have been busy reporting their data too.

An Coimiusiún Pleanála, for example, had a 6.1 per cent gender pay gap in 2025. It’s an improvement of 9.4 per cent on the previous year.

This is down to a relatively higher share of roles taken up by women in administrative grades, which have a lower average hourly pay than other grades, it says.

There are 8 per cent more women than men in the second-from-top pay band, but 12 per cent more men in the top band.

“A great deal of effort [is being made] in recent years to improve our gender balance at senior manager level, including actively supporting family-friendly initiatives such as hybrid working, work sharing, statutory leave schemes and the shorter working year scheme,” says the commission.

The commission reported its 2025 pay gap in three categories – men, women and non-binary – but says the format of the portal makes it impossible to fully report on pay gap statistics for the three groups.

An Post reports a zero gender pay gap for the fifth consecutive year. Its 2025 data shows a mean hourly gender pay gap of minus 4.85 per cent in favour of women. It has an equal percentage of male and female executive directors.

Banking and finance sectors slow to disclose salary information, data shows

Perception

Gender pay gap stats may be particularly beneficial to women in the middle pay quartile, says McDonagh.

“If you can see the norm in your company is for more male representation at the top, maybe you hadn’t realised that’s the context you are working in – the report will tell you that,” says McDonagh.

“Then you are going to have to take charge of your own career, you are going to have to drive it yourself.

“If the stats tell you that men in your organisation have the majority of the income, you are going to have to drive those conversations with your manager yourself to make sure you are getting the opportunity to progress. Keep asking the question, what do I have to do to move up?”

The data is a very public opening of the kimono for organisations, and at a time when HR headcount and diversity and inclusion initiatives are under fire.

“Some 64 per cent of employers have identified employee perception as their biggest concern about publication of their gender pay gap report,” says Adare’s McDonagh of her company’s most recent HR Barometer data.

While gender pay gap statistics can be a bit of a blunt instrument, the statement employers are required to publish explaining the data can be insightful, says McDonagh.

This self-examination requires them to explain the cause of their gender pay gap and what they are going to do about it.

Work to transpose the remaining parts of the European Union (EU) Pay Transparency Directive is continuing, the department says. This will include the obligation for employers to carry out a gender-neutral job evaluation. This requires employers to examine why they are remunerating some types of work more than others. It involves assessing the value of different types of work in their organisation, putting work of similar value into the same category and ensuring these people are similarly paid.

This means equal pay for those doing work of the same value too – even if that work looks quite different.

In UK clothing retailer Next, for example, the mostly female sales staff were found to be earning less than the company’s mostly male warehouse workers. Even though their jobs seem different, the retail staff contributed work of equal value to the warehouse workers, a tribunal found.

Employers will be invited to training to help them compare work objectively – based on skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions – to eliminate gender pay gaps and bias.

Done right, this could upend old pay structures that have unfairly rewarded some skills over others, for no objective reason.

Unlike generics, medicines made from living cells cannot be exactly copied and are referred to ​as biosimilars.

“Ireland could capture a lot more savings ... through greater uptake of the current biosimilars on the market as well as additional biosimilars being introduced,” DiGangi Trench said.

She noted that the ustekinumab drug, which is used in the treatment of psoriasis, had the potential to save the HSE almost €30 million annually, but the uptake here is just 30 per cent against a HSE target of 80 per cent.

The same is true of several other biosimilars, she said.

“A lack of control within the system” meant the potential savings “are just not happening”, she said. In practice that means while some parts of the HSE are utilising the newer lower-cost drugs, others are not.

“Ireland is spending more money than ever on healthcare and in trying to manage that growing pressure ... it could capitalise on more opportunities around biosimilars to reduce its medicines expenditure,” DiGangi Trench said.

She predicted the next decade would be a “golden decade” for biosimilars as the patents on many branded medicines expire.

The company forecasts that approximately $650 billion (€597 billion) worth of branded medicines globally ​are due to lose patent exclusivity between now and 2036. DiGangi Trench compared it to the 2011-2016 patent cliff while noting that Sandoz wants to derive biosimilars from 100 products by 2040.

]]><![CDATA[Why developers are turning to hotels, not apartments]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/why-developers-are-turning-to-hotels-not-apartments/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/why-developers-are-turning-to-hotels-not-apartments/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The cracks are starting to show. After years of defying reality about the Dublin office market’s prospects, developers are now embracing the hotel market as never before.

The latest convert is the German property group KGAL, which wants to knock down an office block on Dublin’s Golden Lane and build a 225-bedroom hotel. They follow in the footsteps of Core Capital’s Derek McGrath and of Johnny Ronan’s eponymous property group, both of which have reversed planned office developments.

The change of heart reflects an anaemic market for office space in Dublin, with CBRE expecting the take-up of office space this year to be roughly in line with last year but below the long-run average. They see a few bright spots on the horizon and tentative signs of the new development cycle, helped somewhat counter-intuitively by demand from artificial intelligence companies.

A more downbeat view is expressed by Peter Keegan, the director of debt and structured finance at CBRE, in a letter submitted to Dublin City Council as part of the KGAL planning application. It can be paraphrased as saying that, notwithstanding the green shoots mentioned above, lenders are wary of office development in Dublin.

Or, as Keegan put it, “there will be much deeper liquidity from debt providers for the development of a hotel on the site versus a new office building ... this is a development which will be received more positively as a hotel project than a speculative office scheme”.

Lenders call the shots in property development, and their enthusiasm for hotel projects is easy to understand. There is a well-documented shortage of hotel rooms in the capital, as evidenced by high occupancy rates. The shortfall is put at 3,600 beds, which equates to 20 or so hotels along the lines of the one planned by KGAL.

The downside with hotels is you have to find someone to run it for you, but if you can get more than 80 per cent occupancy, you will do well. It’s not a one-way bet. About 2,600 new beds are already in the pipeline, according to consultants Mitchell McDermott. The window of opportunity is closing and hence the stampede towards hoteliership by office developers.

From this perspective, their lack of enthusiasm for building apartments is hard to understand given the much larger and open-ended demand – 50,000 homes a year for the foreseeable future.

Again, the KGAL planning application is instructive. It contains an assessment of the site’s potential for an apartment development. The planning report argues that if the various rules and regulations pertaining to apartments – such as access to daylight and minimum open spaces – were to be complied with, then the maximum number of apartments that could be built on the site is between 50 and 60 units. This would not be “viable” even though it is a 10-minute walk from Grafton Street.

The site’s suitability for student accommodation is also deemed not to be “viable”. Urbanest, the student accommodation provider, kindly supplied a letter saying planning constraints “render it not possible” for student accommodation of sufficient scale to be viable. Two-hundred bed spaces would be needed.

Viability gets mentioned a lot in the KGAL planning application, but it is not really defined. Presumably what they are talking about is commercial viability and that is something of movable feast.

It takes a lot of factors into account, including the value of the site for other uses, the costs of construction and the availability and cost of debt financing. It also includes opportunity cost – whether you might make more money using the debt and resources required for Golden Lane elsewhere.

Viability is thus not the same thing as profitability. It may well be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane, but just not as profitable as building a hotel.

Whether it is “viable” to choose an option that delivers a lower profit is another question entirely. It is perfectly reasonable for KGAL to argue it is not viable for them to choose an option – such as apartments instead of a hotel – that will deliver a lower return to their investors.

But that does not mean it would not be viable for someone else with access to cheaper funding and different objectives, such as the Land Development Agency, to build apartments.

Dublin city planners would be doing us some service if they looked a little deeper into the question of viability. Is KGAL saying it would not be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane or simply that it would be more profitable to build a hotel?

The planners might then apply their own definition of viability. It would seem axiomatic that if a 60-unit apartment development could be built at a profit, it would be more than viable from the perspective of the Government’s obligation to house people.

However, those who don’t want telematics to be part of their motor policy can end up paying close to €4,000 for annual cover.

Telematics car insurance uses smart technology to track a driver’s habits through a small device or smartphone app installed in the vehicle.

It monitors metrics such as speed, braking, acceleration and cornering, as well as time spent on the road.

The information is shared with the insurer, and safe drivers are then rewarded with lower premiums.

The system can be particularly useful for young or first-time drivers, or those new to Ireland, who are often hit with penal premiums.

Bonkers.ie sought quotes from a range of providers including AIG, Aviva and Zurich under a number of conditions and found that a 20-year-old driver with a full licence was quoted just €570 for fully comprehensive telematics cover.

When there was no telematics cover, the price of the standard policy jumped to almost €3,900.

What’s driving up the cost of car insurance in Ireland?

Even learner drivers were able to find competitive cover, with a 23-year-old driver with three penalty points quoted €968 for third-party, fire and theft telematics cover, compared with over €2,800 for a standard policy.

“It’s very possible for younger drivers to get on the road for under €1,000 by choosing a telematics policy, especially if they have their full licence,” said Daragh Cassidy from the price comparison site.

He noted that telematics could also benefit drivers who are new to Ireland and don’t have a long record of driving in the country that insurance providers can draw on when deciding on the costs to impose on individual motorists.

Cassidy said that the Bonkers research highlighted how new drivers “shouldn’t automatically rule out getting fully comprehensive cover because they assume it’ll be too expensive. In some cases, a fully comprehensive telematics policy can cost less than a conventional third-party, fire and theft policy.”

He did note, however, that the excesses on some telematics policies can be higher, and he stressed the need to “understand any conditions attached to the cover, including how their driving is monitored and whether there are limits to when and how much they can drive”.

“I’d also encourage parents of young drivers to take note of our findings,” Cassidy said.

“Many first-time drivers will rely on the ‘bank of mum and dad’ to help them get on the road. So for parents worried about facing a four-figure insurance bill for their son or daughter, telematics is certainly worth investigating.”

Last week, Netflix announced it had bought the rights to all 104 matches of the 2030 World Cup in Spain, which co-hosts the tournament with Portugal and Morocco. The price wasn’t disclosed. Why the change of heart? Partly because Netflix and its rivals have run out of easy growth in mature markets. Keeping existing subscribers is just as important as finding new ones, and sport is the most reliable antidote for churn. People who binge a drama often cancel when it ends, but people who follow a team tend to stay for the whole season.

Then there’s advertising. Every big streamer now offers a cheaper tier carrying ads, and advertisers will pay a premium for audiences watching live in large numbers simultaneously. The economics of sports rights explains why the price keeps rising inexorably. A league or federation sells something that cannot be replicated by a new entrant (no matter how hard the Saudis try). Rights are carved up by territory, by package and by platform to maximise the number of bidders. Those bidders need the property so badly that they overpay for it. The pay-TV model that Sky built around the Premier League in the 1990s established the principle of sport as the anchor holding an expensive bundle together.

Now the bundle is fraying. According to Ampere Analysis, streaming services will spend about $14.2 billion on sports rights this year. Amazon has overtaken DAZN as the biggest spender, and general entertainment platforms like Amazon, Netflix, Disney+, Apple and Paramount+ now account for 44 per cent of the total, up from 31 per cent last year. Their advantage over a specialist like DAZN, which has lost billions acquiring and distributing rights across Europe and Japan, is that sport doesn’t have to pay for itself. Make it easier to watch live sport in one place and you’ll do away with dodgy boxes

Free-to-air sport in Ireland is not going away. The designated list remains a protection, and RTÉ still has the reach that rights holders and sponsors value. But the new bidding war is changing the calculus. The streamers are bigger, richer and more strategically focused than the satellite companies ever were, and they’re no longer content to view live sport as an optional extra.

Government can solve most of the problems with “the stroke of a pen”, according to the industry advocate, who adds that they are largely the result of policy.

Data centres are not allowed to start operations without national grid connections, for which they have to wait five years, even while they must have their own electricity supplies, Kelly maintains.

His organisation wants this rule changed to allow centres to start operations using their own power sources, on condition that they immediately connect to the grid once that is possible.

Alongside this, data centres cannot count renewable power supplied through direct connections to wind or solar plants, known as private lines, against the 80 per cent requirement, which can only be met with green electricity from the grid.

Data centres could meet their renewable commitments quickly if they were allowed to count what they buy through private lines, Kelly argues.

This would also provide an outlet for wind and solar plants that are often prevented by a lack of capacity in parts of the national grid from supplying electricity to the market.

‘Big tech’s lapdog’: How can we break free from the sector’s malign influence?

DII argues that concerns that data centres will draw natural gas supplies away from new housing ignore the fact that policy dictates that new homes will use electricity.

The organisation has no difficulty with many aspects of the rules now governing data centre connection, stresses Kelly, who adds that the Republic has stricter regulations governing the industry than many jurisdictions.

Their presence here is a result of long-standing policy, he says. Government built the telecoms lines they needed in the late ‘90s. “We built the infrastructure and lo and behold, they came,” he says.

]]>cybrain<![CDATA[Social-housing pilot guarantees rent for landlords – but will they sign up?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/guaranteed-rent-on-offer-for-landlords-but-will-they-sign-up/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/guaranteed-rent-on-offer-for-landlords-but-will-they-sign-up/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000A new pilot scheme, aimed at boosting the supply of social housing by offering a “secure, low-risk letting option” for landlords, has been launched by the Department of Housing.

Run by councils across Dublin for now, if it’s a success, it might be rolled out across the State.

Announcing the Dublin Rental Accommodation Scheme pilot scheme earlier this year, Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage James Browne said: “By encouraging more landlords to make their properties available, the pilot will help increase the supply of homes for individuals and families in need of social housing”.

But how does it work? Is it attractive for landlords? And with the rental market so tight, is it going to be enough to get landlords to commit to social housing?

Run on a pilot basis across the four Dublin local authority areas, the new rental accommodation scheme is being pitched as a “flexible, secure and financially attractive way to let residential properties”.

The tenant target is households that have received rent supplement for 18 months or more, and that have an ongoing housing need. The tenant pays an income-based differential rent contribution to the local authority, and the local authority pays the landlord the agreed rent.

The hope is that if more private landlords sign up for the scheme, more properties should become available to social housing tenants.

What’s different?

This is not the first time councils have looked to incentivise landlords to let their properties through local authorities. The rental accommodation scheme has two components – one working through approved housing boards letting their properties to councils and the other a private-sector arrangement whereby private landlords enter into rental agreements with local authorities.

It is the latter that the new pilot scheme is focusing on.

There have been challenges in attracting and retaining enough properties through the previous scheme. According to a review from the Department of Housing back in 2025, there has been a significant decline in the number of private landlords participating in it.

In 2023, for example, 1,004 landlords left the scheme but just 103 entered, leaving 7,010 tenancies. This compares to 11,231 back in 2018.

Three reasons for this are cited in the report: landlords selling the unit; tenants allocated social housing; and the landlord didn’t renew the contract.

And there are fewer landlords signing up, for reasons including rents on offer that are below market levels.

A spokeswoman for the Irish Property Owners Association (IPOA) says the scheme was “disadvantaged from the start” due to the rules set out in rent pressure zones. The maximum landlords could set rents at through the rental accommodation scheme was 92 per cent of market rent but this made it difficult to get back to a market rate, as only specified increases were allowed.

“It ended up that landlords were actually stuck with that sub-market rate due to rent pressure zones, which made the rent accommodation scheme unappealing,” she says.

HAP (housing assistance payment), on the other hand, had no such limits on the level rent was set at, as councils contribute a fixed amount and the tenant tops up the gap. This made it more attractive to landlords.

As a result, the new rent accommodation scheme pilot has been launched with some key differences. Firstly, landlords can charge local authorities up to 100 per cent of market rent. This rent is guaranteed, and will be paid “in full and on time” by the local authority – not the tenant.

And, if a tenant decides to leave, the council will pay the rent until a new tenant is placed.

Moreover, tenants will be sourced by the local authority, which means landlords won’t have to take on the task of vetting possible tenants.

The maximum length of a contract has also been extended, from four-to-six years previously to eight under the pilot scheme.

Rental payments will be front-loaded, so landlords won’t have to wait for their first payment. There will be better damage and compensation arrangements. And applications for the scheme will be more streamlined. Landlords will be responsible for managing the tenancy, and the property.

Is it enough?

County councils certainly hope it is. Pamela Kearns, mayor of South Dublin County Council, says the scheme will transform lives.

“Every property made available provides a vulnerable family, individual or senior with a safe, stable home in our community. While Dublin desperately needs housing, it also thrives on collaboration. Landlords now have a meaningful way to tackle housing shortages and build stronger communities. It is a true win for owners, tenants and Dublin as a whole.”

Already there has been “significant” interest in the new pilot, says the Department of Housing, with about 200 applications received by the end of September.

However, while the new scheme may have some key differences, groups representing property owners say it may not be enough to encourage landlords out of the private market and into guaranteed rent through the rental accommodation scheme.

“It looks very well on paper, but once you scratch the surface it’s not really like that,” says the spokeswoman for the IPOA, adding that there are a “couple of hurdles” that are making it unpalatable for landlords.

Firstly, the promise of full market rent is a “marketing strategy”, says the spokeswoman, because under the current legislation, a landlord can only charge market rent if they’re eligible for it, such as at the end of a six-year tenancy cycle. And if you’re not eligible then the council cannot override Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) rules.

Another issue is the length of the contract. A contract of a maximum eight years could mean that smaller landlords (ie those with four or fewer properties) could end up with a tenant for 12 years – even if the council drops out after eight. And larger landlords could have the tenant for life even if the council is no longer involved.

And if the tenancy wasn’t working out, such as if the tenant stopped paying rent, the IPOA spokeswoman says the landlord would need to go down the standard legal route, and issue a notice of termination. But it can take up to two years to get vacant possession of the property, she says.

However, the spokesman for the Department of Housing says tenancies can match up and “a six-year rent accommodation scheme agreement can align with the statutory cycle for small landlords with one to three tenancies, provided the relevant start dates coincide”.

For larger tenants, however, these new tenancies can only be ended for breaches of tenant obligations or because the property no longer meets the needs of the household’s accommodation needs.

Another challenge that might arise is that although the landlord doesn’t select their tenant, if things go wrong, they still have to sort it out. “The main landlord-tenant relationship ultimately remains the same between the property owner and the rental accommodation scheme tenant as it would with a typical private rented tenancy,” the scheme’s documentation states.

Forward payment is just two months, while other benefits can’t really be described as such, the IPOA argues. The offer of “100 per cent mortgage interest tax relief” is something all landlords are entitled to – while property tax is not eligible for a tax deduction.

Another factor, says the spokeswoman, is that the rental accommodation scheme has “very, very strict property standards enforcement”.

If an issue is identified – and according to the spokeswoman it could be something as relatively minor as the width set on window restrictors – rent payments will be suspended until the landlord gets its sorted.

The scheme is being run on a pilot basis until 2029 to see whether or not this additional flexibility will result in an increased flow of properties.

“This pilot allows us to test whether additional flexibility and stronger supports can increase property owner participation and expand the supply of homes available to social housing tenants,” the Minister said, adding that the results of the scheme would guide future national policy.

]]><![CDATA[Did the budget help a widow with two young children?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/did-the-budget-help-a-widow-with-two-young-children/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/did-the-budget-help-a-widow-with-two-young-children/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000I am a widow with two young children, in my second year of widowhood. I am in a good job and lucky enough to be able to support the three of us, even with reduced working hours.

I pay a significant amount of tax through my PAYE as the widow’s pension gets taxed that way. My take-home pay was significantly more when we were jointly assessed as a couple and I was caring for my sick husband.

Does the recent budget help the solo parent families from a tax viewpoint? And, where I lose out as one earner, is there any improvement to the social welfare support for me? Little has changed in our outgoings since four became three, and those kids are getting bigger and hungrier.

GM

Raising children is tough enough. Raising them on your own after having had to care for your husband when he was ill is a daunting challenge.

It’s at times like this that you hope a budget will deal a decisive blow in your favour, but, unfortunately for you and others who are financially vulnerable, this Government has sought to spread its largesse thinly and widely – hardly helped by the hospitality VAT cut last year limiting its room for manoeuvre this time around.

To make matters worse, although an exceptional tax credit is granted to new widows with children to try to ease the blow of two earners becoming one or the loss of joint assessment, the credit is phased down every year. And it does not appear to have been adjusted in the budget.

Although it will have been worth €3,600 to you the year after you were widowed, this drops to €3,150 in the second year of widowhood, €2,700 in year three, €2,250 in year four and €1,800 in year five.

This is on top of the annual widow’s tax credit, which replaces whatever other personal tax credit you might have been on previously. It is payable at €2,000 this year.

Leaving shares to a spouse at death can make more sense than a lifetime transfer

This credit tends to keep pace with the single person’s tax credit so I am assuming it rises next year to €2,125.

You should also be eligible for the single person child carer credit as long as your children are under 18 or in full-time education over that age. It is worth €1,900 this year, but will rise to €2,025 next year.

You refer to the widow’s pension and you are certainly eligible for that. On the basis of what you say, you will be on the contributory pension – a payment that is available to you because of your PRSI record or your husband’s. In your case, I am assuming it is on the basis of your record.

I should say this pension has now been renamed the bereaved partner’s (contributory) pension. It’s not just because someone in social protection decided the word “widow” needed changing: the pension is, since last year, now available also to cohabiting couples where one partner has died.

If they don’t have children, they must have been together for five years, or, for those with dependent children, two years.

Widows under the age of 66 get between €252.60 and €259.50 weekly, depending on the number of PRSI stamps they have. Those over the age of 66 get a payment of between €286.60 and €299.30.

If, like you, they have dependent children, they get €58 a week for each child under the age of 12 and €78 for older children.

Anyway, along with most other welfare payments, this payment will rise by €10 from January of next year. So, if you are on the maximum payment for someone under 66, it will rise to €269.50 a week. And the payments for children rise by €6 a week – to €64 or €84 depending on the age of your children.

As a result, you will get an additional €22 a week, or just shy of €1,150 a year, unless one of your children turns 12 next year. It’s not nothing, but if, as you say, you are paying tax on this money, it doesn’t really stretch too far.

If your children are in childcare or after-school care with a creche that is signed up to the Government’s core funding model, that cost will come down next year but not until September.

On top of that, you will also benefit from the employee or earned income tax credit, which is rising by €125 a year to €2,125.

Is my €1,000 monthly childcare bill really falling to €550?

There is also a benefit from the widening of the standard rate income tax band. As a widow, you pay 20 per cent income tax up to €48,000, which is better than the €44,000 for a single person, but short of the €53,000 you would have had as a married couple with one person working.

From January, your 20 per cent band will increase to €50,500, which will cut your tax bill by €500 as long as you are earning above that €50,500 level.

On the flip side, PRSI is rising for all employees although there will be a modest cut in your Universal Social Charge.

All told, you will be around €950 better off next year, leaving aside childcare, which may or may not be relevant.

]]><![CDATA[Ex-Labour Court chairman subject to dignity-at-work complaint from senior official, WRC told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/ex-labour-court-chairman-subject-to-dignity-at-work-complaint-from-senior-official-wrc-hears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/ex-labour-court-chairman-subject-to-dignity-at-work-complaint-from-senior-official-wrc-hears/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:56:35 +0000A former chairman of the Labour Court was the subject of a dignity-at-work complaint by an ordinary member of the court who has now claimed unfair dismissed, the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) has heard

The complainant, Peter DR Murphy, who sat as a member of the Labour Court from 2005 to 2024 as a nominee of business group Ibec, is pursuing allegations of unfair dismissal and other rights breaches against the Minister for Enterprise.

The State said Ibec did not nominate Murphy for a further term after his last warrant expired in 2024. Murphy’s legal team has said the department did not seek replacement nominees from the business group when the warrant ran out.

Murphy, a qualified solicitor, had been earning more than €140,000 a year in the role.

He alleged he was subject to workplace bullying during his appointment and he specifically identified a former chairman in a formal dignity-at-work complaint, according to legal correspondence in 2020 opened to a hearing on Monday.

Tara Coogan, a civil servant at the Department of Enterprise who was in charge of the section overseeing the Labour Court and the WRC at the end of Murphy’s last term on the court, gave evidence on the respondent’s preliminary objection to the case going ahead on Monday.

Frances Meenan, for the State, asked Coogan about a legal letter of October 5th, 2020, to former minister for enterprise Damien English from the complainants’ former solicitors.

In the letter, read out by Coogan, Murphy’s then solicitors wrote: “Our client has grave concerns about recent steps regarding the renewal of his warrant.”

The alleged change in practice was “not coincidental and is a direct response to certain recent events and issues raised by our client in respect of his working conditions and the treatment he has been forced to endure in the workplace”, the letter also said.

The letter stated Murphy had raised statutory claims concerning “bullying, victimisation and other related matters” and had “also instituted internal complaint against the chairman of the Labour Court under the Civil Service dignity at work policy”.

At that point, Meenan intervened and said: “We won’t mention any names.”

Coogan said: “I don’t know anything about this letter.”

Meenan said the State would present evidence that the complaints referenced in the letter “were subsequently withdrawn by the complainant”.

Tiernan Lowey, for the complainant, said: “We’re happy for the letter to be read out in full.”

The tribunal has heard how Murphy received one further term on the court before his final warrant lapsed in February 2024.

Meenan said it was position of the State that Murphy was not an employee and therefore had no standing to pursue the claim.

She said appointment to the Labour Court was contingent on Murphy being put forward as a nominee by Ibec, and accordingly Murphy’s 19 years at the Labour Court came to an end, Meenan said.

However, Lowey said: “We don’t believe there ever was any correspondence from the department or on behalf of the department [to Ibec] when Murphy’s last warrant expired.”

Lowey said Murphy “was never regarded as anything other than an employee of the minister”. The complainant’s position is that it had become the custom and practice to renew warrants until a member of the court resigned and only then seek three nominees.

Meenan accepted the State had “a gap” in its supporting documentation as copies of correspondence between the department and Ibec asking the employers’ group to put forward a nominee for the court every time Murphy had been reappointed were not with its legal papers.

She said the documents in question were “old paper files that are hard to get”.

Adjudicator Christina Ryan said it was “unusual” that the State was not ready with the documents in question when it was making the nomination process a “central feature” of its case.

She directed the State to produce the material and said the matter could be revisited when the case resumed on Wednesday.

Murphy’s complaints are under the Unfair Dismissals Act, the Protection of Employees (Fixed-Term Work) Act, the Redundancy Payments Act and the Minimum Notice and Terms of Employment Act.

]]>Collins Photos<![CDATA[Student accommodation plan for Dublin’s Blackpitts gets green light]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/01/28/student-accommodation-plan-for-dublins-blackpitts-gets-green-light/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/01/28/student-accommodation-plan-for-dublins-blackpitts-gets-green-light/Wed, 28 Jan 2026 16:52:32 +0000An Coimisiún Pleanála has given the green light for plans by businessman Eamon Waters for a purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) for Blackpitts, in Dublin 8, despite local opposition.

Mr Waters’ Blackpitts Residence UC was seeking planning permission for a 217-student bed space across six floors.

However, the planning commission has ordered the omission of a proposed fifth floor containing 28 bed spaces, which reduces the overall scheme to 189 bed spaces.

The ruling upheld a decision by the city council, which also ordered the omission of the fifth floor, and Blackpitts Residence UC appealed against that condition.

The removal of the fifth floor was ordered in order to protect visual and residential amenity and prevent undue impact on neighbouring properties.

McGill Planning, on behalf of Blackpitts Residence UC, said that the omission of the fifth floor would “not only diminish the design quality, while delivering no tangible planning or amenity benefit, but it will also negatively impact the commercial viability of the project as a Dublin city PBSA for institutional investment”.

The scheme was also the source of a political row last October when the Minister for Further and Higher Education, James Lawless, wrote to Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald to complain about Sinn Féin councillor Ciarán Ó Meachair opposing the scheme.

In his submission to the council, Mr Ó Meachair said that “we have an over-concentration of PBSAs in Dublin 8 already. The new proposal would be the 10th such development here since 2017 and 13 PBSAs in total.”

Mr Ó Meachair claimed that “the overabundance of hotels, student accommodations and short-term rentals have hollowed out much of the sense of community in the Liberties”.

Eamon Waters’ firm appeals ‘unreasonable’ limits on student housing development in Dublin 8

Two third-party appeals by Peter Crotty of Hammond Street, Blackpitts, and Anita Kenna were also lodged against the scheme.

In her appeal, Ms Kenna, a local resident, told the commission that she moved to the Liberties, which she describes one of Dublin’s most welcoming and neighbourly areas, and her goal was to integrate and “make this my long-term home”.

She said: “However, now that I am surrounded by short-term rental, hotels and transient accommodation blocks, that sense of neighbourhood has been lost. It is extremely disheartening to realise that this may no longer be my ‘forever home’.”

The inspector in the case, Katy Tuck, recommended that planning permission be granted after concluding that the scheme “would constitute an acceptable scale and density of development in this urban location and would not seriously injure the residential or visual amenities of the area or properties in the vicinity”.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445740/">
   <title>Stocker zu Kontakten mit Pilnacek befragt</title>
   <description>Im parlamentarischen U-Ausschuss zur Causa Christian Pilnacek ist am Mittwoch Bundeskanzler Christian Stocker (ÖVP) befragt worden. Im Fokus standen Kontakte mit dem später verstorbenen Ex-Justizsektionschef während der Zeit Stockers als ÖVP-Generalsekretär. Vorgelegt wurden Passagen aus dem Auswertungsbericht der Wirtschafts- und Korruptionsstaatsanwaltschaft (WKStA) zu Pilnaceks Daten, der auch direkte Korrespondenzen beinhaltet.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3445740/</link>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445771/">
   <title>Sicherheitslücken bedrohen Websites</title>
   <description>Zwei am Mittwoch einer großen Öffentlichkeit bekanntgewordene schwere Sicherheitslücken mit großem Schadpotenzial haben weltweit für Aufregung gesorgt. Zahlreiche Institutionen schalteten vorsorglich ihre Websites ab. Betroffen ist die weit verbreitete Programmiersprache PHP. Die Entwickler kündigten bereits an, dass eine neue Version zur Behebung der Sicherheitslücken verfügbar sei. Sie appellierten an alle Nutzer und Nutzerinnen, das Update sofort durchzuführen.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3445771/</link>
   <dc:subject>IT</dc:subject>
   <dc:date>2026-10-21T17:30:54+02:00</dc:date>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445757/">
   <title>Aussichten auf neue Dreiergespräche</title>
   <description>Nach Gesprächen mit dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj am Dienstag in Oslo hat der US-Gesandte Steve Witkoff Russlands Präsidenten Wladimir Putin am Mittwoch in St. Petersburg getroffen. Dabei habe er ihm Vorschläge und „Ideen“ für einen Friedenspakt vorgelegt. Der Kreml zeigte sich „im Prinzip“ zu neuen Gesprächen mit der Ukraine und den USA bereit. Zugleich kündigte Moskau erste Diesellieferungen an die USA an und meldete die Freilassung des US-Bürgers Stephen Hubbard.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3445757/</link>
   <dc:subject>Ausland</dc:subject>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445736/">
   <title>Rubio bringt bei Drosselung Musk ins Spiel</title>
   <description>Für Ungemach zwischen der Ukraine und den USA sorgt weiterhin eine Drosselung des für die ukrainische Abwehr notwendigen Satellitennetzwerks Starlink von Elon Musk. US-Außenminister Marco Rubio sagte am Mittwoch, dass Entscheidungen über den Zugang der Ukraine zum Satellitennetzwerk beim Betreiber SpaceX und dessen Chef Musk liegen. Die Äußerungen kommen einer Kehrtwende in der Argumentation der US-Regierung gleich.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445712/">
   <title>Geisterfahrt im Fokus</title>
   <description>Mit der Befragung zweier Polizeibeamter ist am Mittwoch der parlamentarische Untersuchungsausschuss zur Causa Christian Pilnacek fortgesetzt worden. Im Fokus stand die Geisterfahrt des ehemaligen Justizsektionschefs in der Nacht vor dessen Tod am 20. Oktober 2023. Am Nachmittag ist Bundeskanzler Christian Stocker (ÖVP) geladen, der damals Generalsekretär der Volkspartei war. Die FPÖ teilte unterdessen mit, dass der U-Ausschuss um drei Monate verlängert wird.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445728/">
   <title>Alice Schwarzer stellt „Emma“ ein</title>
   <description>Alice Schwarzer stellt ihr feministisches Magazin „Emma“ ein. „Nach 50 Jahren und 398 Ausgaben mit 36.584 Seiten verlässt ‚Emma‘ die Bühne“, teilte die Journalistin und Frauenrechtlerin am Mittwoch in Köln mit. Die letzte Ausgabe erscheint im Dezember. „Emma“ werde nicht aus ökonomischen Gründen eingestellt, wie Schwarzer betonte, „nein, wir gehen, weil wir meinen: Es reicht“.</description>

   <title>Witkoff bei Putin in St. Petersburg</title>
   <description>Nach Gesprächen mit dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj in Oslo ist US-Unterhändler Steve Witkoff Mittwochfrüh zu Gesprächen mit der russischen Führung in St. Petersburg eingetroffen. Witkoff legte Russland von den Europäern und Amerikanern erarbeitete Vorschläge für eine Friedenslösung im russischen Angriffskrieg vor. Poland has condemned a decision by the Lviv region in Ukraine to declare 2027 a year honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led the massacre of Poles during World War Two, and one of its leaders, Roman Shukhevych.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland.

Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska.

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 20, 2026

On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN).

Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice.

The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander.

While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children.

 

Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw.

“Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska.

“Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves.

Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”.

The European Parliament has criticised Ukraine's @ZelenskyyUa for naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII, calling it an "unprovoked escalation" that is “not in line with European values” and "disregards Polish sensitivities" https://t.co/54rbPSrs9S

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

 

On Wednesday, Tusk said that such decisions “harm Ukraine” by “making the work of Ukraine’s friends and supporters of closer cooperation very difficult”. By contrast, the “Russians always rub their hands in glee in situations like these”, added Tusk, quoted by Polsat News.

Meanwhile, Sikorski announced that he had signed a motion to place Sheremeta, who has led the efforts to commemorate the UPA and Shukhevych in Lviv, on Poland’s “list of undesirable persons”.

Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine.

Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.…

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026

Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”.

It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.”

However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN.

The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M.

Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz

— Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026

Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession.

However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory.

But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”.

Since then, tensions have calmed, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan that includes approving more exhumations. This month, the head of the IPN and its Ukrainian counterpart held their first meeting since 2018.

]]> Parliament approves liberalisation of Poland’s abortion laws https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/21/parliament-approves-liberalisation-of-polands-abortion-laws/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:41:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105798

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis.
To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok.
Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.

.@BoguckiZbigniew o stanowisku prezydenta ws. aborcji ⬇️

🗨️ Pan prezydent w tej kampanii mówił, że jest za ochroną życia od poczęcia do naturalnej śmierci@GoscWydarzen 🎙️ @mtejchmanhttps://t.co/ZJ4gKAPywM

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 20, 2026

A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS.

Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year.

Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law.

]]> Polish leaders condemn Hegseth’s “scandalous” remarks downplaying role of US allies in Afghanistan https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/20/polish-leaders-condemn-hegseths-scandalous-remarks-downplaying-role-of-us-allies-in-afghanistan/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 19:52:13 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105772

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Leading figures from Poland’s ruling coalition have hit back at US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth over his recent remarks downplaying the contribution of America’s allies during the war in Afghanistan.

The speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, called the comments “scandalous”, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk read out a message sent to him by a Polish army medic who was serving in Afghanistan when the last of 44 Polish soldiers who died there was declared dead.

💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️

Chciałbym, żeby te słowa dotarły do naszych sojuszników, żeby już nigdy więcej nikt nie lekceważył wysiłku naszych żołnierzy. pic.twitter.com/gGJkh4Gnft

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 20, 2026

The controversy stemmed from a speech the US defence secretary gave to US military cadets in Tennessee on Saturday. Hegseth referred to his time serving as a US Army officer in Afghanistan, where he recalled that the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) headquarters had flags from over 50 countries.

“Except,” Hegseth said, “there were maybe five [countries] that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually, by the end, were involved in kinetic operations. In fact, the patch ‘ISAF’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting.'”

The comments earned quick reproach from Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, who aimed a message at Hegseth on social media, saying: “Tell that to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province.”

Tell that, Mr @SecWar, to the families of 44 Polish soldiers who died securing the tough Ghazni province. https://t.co/vm4TM0sMJO

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 18, 2026

On Tuesday, the remarks earned even stronger reproach from Czarzasty, who is the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, and the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of the groups that forms Poland’s ruling coalition.

At a press conference, Czarzasty said that Hegseth’s “scandalous” comments are “harmful to the families of Polish soldiers and to Polish national pride”.

He also criticised President Karol Nawrocki – an opponent of the government and conservative ally of Donald Trump – for not condemning Hegseth’s remarks.

It is “an insult to Polish soldiers” that Nawrocki, who serves as commander-in-chief, “is unable to stand up for their dignity and the dignity of those who died”, declared Czarzasty.

To skandaliczne, że prezydent Polski boi się potępić polityków amerykańskich za brak szacunku do polskich żołnierzy, którzy zginęli w Afganistanie. pic.twitter.com/uyv54yDvrI

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) October 20, 2026

Later on Tuesday, Tusk read out to his cabinet a text message he said he had received from a former military medic, whom he did not name.

“Please stand up for soldiers, I beg you,” wrote the medic. “During my tour in Afghanistan, we confirmed the death of the last Polish casualty, a platoon sergeant whose wife was pregnant in Poland at the time.”

“I received a medal from the Americans for helping them, for treating Americans. I didn’t have to do that. We treated them with our own Polish medicines,” they added.

Tusk then added his own remarks, stating: “I would like these words to reach our allies. So that no one will ever again downplay the efforts of our soldiers. Wherever our allies, including our closest ally, the Americans, have needed our participation, Polish soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with them.”

Tusk also referenced Nawrocki’s silence on the matter. “Frankly, I was also counting on the president speaking out on this matter. But it seems I miscalculated.”

 

Tusk is the first European head of government to directly criticise Hegseth’s remarks, although a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham did say on Monday that it was “wrong to diminish the role” of British personnel, 457 of whom died in Afghanistan.

Of the 3,621 coalition deaths during the war in Afghanistan, around two thirds were Americans (2,461). The rest came from 31 different countries, with Poland’s 44 fatalities the seventh most of any nation.

Hegseth’s remarks are not the first time that the Trump administration has caused anger in Poland by downplaying allies’ role in Afghanistan. In January, Trump himself suggested that other countries had “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines”.

That prompted General Roman Polko, who commanded Poland’s GROM special forces unit in Iraq and Afghanistan, to call the US president “a coward who has never been on the front lines”.

The former commander of Poland's special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan has condemned Donald Trump for questioning the contribution of America's allies

"This is the cynicism of a coward who hasn’t been on the front lines himself," said General @PolkoRoman https://t.co/kElkAO5qX4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 23, 2026

The Polish government has also clashed with the US on other issues. In January, Tusk joined other European leaders in calling for Greenland’s sovereignty to be respected, following Trump’s calls for the island to be brought under US control.

The following month, Tusk declared that Poland would not be a “vassal” of the US and suggested that Nawrocki wanted Poland to be too subservient to Washington. Czarzasty has twice this year clashed with the US ambassador over critical remarks he made towards Trump.

However, at the same time, the Polish government has sought to maintain positive relations with Washington, given the United States’ role as Poland’s most important security partner. In June, Poland formally requested that the US establish a new permanent military base on its territory.

Hegseth himself has praised Poland, calling it a “model ally” last year. The US State Department this month also announced that it was pushing for Poland to be allowed to join the G20 “as soon as possible”, pointing to its “growing leadership position in the international arena”.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.

However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.

“Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily.
