Across five studies of secondhand-market haggling, sellers were often more candid than buyers expected. Three minutes of small talk before the haggling narrowed the gap, and so did asking buyers to think about the seller's conscience first.]]>

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

Chronic offense-taking isn't performative outrage—it's a trauma response masquerading as oversensitivity.]]>

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

The news comes as Agility inches closer to its IPO via SPAC and after it announced the latest version of Digit. | Source: Agility Robotics

AGCO and Agility Robotics have signed a commercial agreement to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid in AGCO’s manufacturing facility. The U.S. pilot, expected to begin in 2027, will support AGCO’s efforts to create more flexible, intelligent factories, beginning at its production site in Hesston, Kan.

“This strategic relationship views humanoid robotics and AI as essential ’teammates‘ in building flexible, intelligent factories,” stated Thomas Enghof, director of manufacturing technology at AGCO. “They unlock automation in complex, human-centric workflows, augmenting human capabilities by absorbing repetitive, strenuous or hazardous tasks. By pairing human ingenuity with robust robotic engineering and strict safety governance, we create resilient manufacturing systems that empower the workforce and deliver measurable business value.”

AGCO said it is a global leader in agricultural machinery and precision agriculture technologies. The Duluth, Ga.-based company‘s brands include Fendt, Massey Ferguson, PTx, and Valtra. AGCO said its high-performance equipment and smart farming systems, including brand-agnostic retrofit technologies and autonomous offerings, “empower farmers to drive productivity while sustainably feeding the world.”

AGCO joins a growing list of Digit deployments

Digit uses AI to continuously learn and adapt to evolving workflows, enabling greater operational flexibility and improved productivity, according to Agility. When paired with the Agility Arc cloud-based platform for deploying and managing robot fleets, companies can rapidly integrate automation into essential operations without requiring extensive infrastructure changes or costly facility upgrades, it added.

AGCO joins a growing number of global leading companies deploying Agility’s humanoid robots, including Toyota, GXO Logistics, and Schaeffler.

“We’re excited to work alongside AGCO as they continue to lead the way in agricultural innovation,” said Daniel Diez, chief business officer of Agility. “By introducing Agility’s Digit humanoid robots into AGCO’s operations, we have an opportunity to strengthen manufacturing processes, support employees in demanding tasks, and demonstrate how advanced robotics can create measurable impact across modern production environments.”

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Agility is on the move

Agility said its humanoid robot will initially support key assembly and production operations including sorting and stacking parts sorting, as well as intelligent placement of totes for storage. The physical AI company asserted that Digit will enhance ergonomic safety, improve operational efficiency, and empower employees to focus on higher-value, skill-driven work that advances innovation and productivity.

It has been a busy time for Agility Robotics. Last month, the company unveiled the latest version of its robot, Digit 5. The latest version of Digit includes new legs, upgraded batteries, and a more comprehensive safety architecture. The Salem, Ore.-based company also recently confirmed that it is exploring building wheeled robots for its customers.

Agility is preparing to become a public company through its previously announced merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The business combination is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, after which the combined company will operate as Agility Robotics and is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “AGLT.”

Deepu Talla, NVIDIA’s VP of robotics and edge AI, gave the opening talk at RoboBusiness 2025.

RoboBusiness 2026 will come to an end today. After a packed first day of the 20th anniversary show, here is everything you need to know about Day 2.

The second day of RoboBusiness will start at 9:30 a.m. PT with the “State of Humanoids” panel. During this keynote, industry leaders will explore the capabilities humanoids are delivering today, the technical and operational challenges that remain, and the lessons emerging from early industrial implementations. All keynotes will take place in the theater on the second floor.

This panel will include insights from Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer of Agility Robotics; Parker Conroy, the head of product management at Apptronik; Michael Patrick Perry, head of commercial strategy at Persona AI; Aadeel Akhtar, the founder and CEO of PSYONIC. Mike Oitzman, senior editor at The Robot Report, will host the panel.

The Exhibitor Hall will open at 10:00 a.m. and stay open until 3:00 p.m. There, attendees can find interesting robotics demos and the Startup Alley.

We’ll be closing RoboBusiness 2026 with a final keynote talk at 3:00 p.m. Morgan Pope, the director of companionship at Familiar Machines & Magic, will lead a session on how the startup is creating robotic characters.

Registration for the show is available on site.

Morning breakout session schedule

Breakout sessions will start after the morning keynote and a short networking break. RoboBusiness 2026 sessions starting at 10:45 a.m. include:

  • Egocentric Robot Learning: Teaching Robots Through Human Experience: Ted Larson, co-founder and CEO of OLogic, will explore the foundations of egocentric robot learning, the technical challenges involved in building these systems, and their implications for the future of commercial robotics. His talk will be in Room 203.
  • China’s Physical AI Ecosystem in 2026: Competitor, Supplier, Benchmark: Georg Stieler, managing director for Asia at Stieler Technology, will share the latest insights from his company’s work on the ground in China and put them into global perspective. The session will be in Room 207.
  • An Introduction to Robotic Tools for Overhead Power Line Operations: Trevor Anderson, the chief strategy officer at FulcrumAir, will examine mobilization, installation precision, live-line capabilities and opportunities to complete work without helicopters or required outages. The talk will take place in Room 209/210.
  • Precision, Power, Perception: Enabling Next-Gen Humanoid Actuation: Jordan Grotz, senior robotics systems engineer at Allegro MicroSystems, will dissect the critical technological advancements that are making next-generation robotic actuation possible. He will speak in Room 206.
  • Why Physical AI Fails in the Real World: This panel will include insights from SK Gupta, co-founder and chief scientist of GrayMatter Robotics; Brian Geisel, founder and CEO of Geisel Software & Symage; and Sparsh Gautam, a computer vision engineer at Tesla. They will discuss how teams are addressing challenges across perception, decision-making, and manipulation to create robots that can operate safely and predictably outside the lab. The session will be in Room 204.

Sessions starting at 11:45 a.m. include:

  • Building Physical AI that Scales: Dermot O’Driscoll, vice president of go-to-market physical AI at Arm, will examine key compute principles behind trusted physical AI, including how intelligence is distributed across cloud and edge compute and the coordination of learned and deterministic behaviors. He will also explain how developers can design systems that remain adaptable, reliable, and safe as they scale to production. The talk will be in Room 203.
  • Reshoring With Robots: A Policy Discussion: This panel discussion will include insights from Ellie Sakhaee, an AI policy manager at Google; Dr. Henrik I Christensen, a distinguished professor of computer science at UC San Diego; Brendan Schulman, vice president of policy and government relations at Boston Dynamics; and Michael Bearman, the chief legal and safety officer at Vecna Robotics. The group will examine the need for a national robotics strategy and debate industrial priorities. Eugene Demaitre, editorial director for The Robot Report, will moderate this session in Room 207.
  • SparkE-B: Building a Robot for Safer Electrical Work:  Yakov Bobrov, co-founder and chief technology officer of Hardhat Robotics, will explore the challenges of deploying robots in dynamic construction environments, the engineering behind safety-critical robotic systems, and how AI-enabled autonomy could help skilled tradespeople dramatically increase productivity. The talk will take place in Room 209/210.
  • The Dexterous Hand: Delivering Force and Signal via Synthetic Tendons: Jim Hotary, VP of technology at Maeden Innovation, will examine key engineering challenges including fatigue life, creep, abrasion resistance, friction management, routing constraints, and reliability under millions of flex cycles. His session will be in Room 206.
  • Human-Robot Interaction: Bridging Academia and Industry: Fraz Yousuf, a senior robotics application engineer at Eli Lilly, will share what they learned running HRI field studies with manufacturing and warehouse operators around live AGVs, some early findings of people’s perception of robots on the manufacturing floor and the playbook they built to make the partnership repeatable. This talk will take place in Room 204.

RoboBusiness 2026 features more afternoon sessions

Breakout sessions starting at 2:00 p.m. include:

  • Real-Time Robot Troubleshooting with AI Agents and MCP: Rohit John Varghese, the director of systems engineering and product at Contoro Robotics, will give an introduction to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and then show examples on a real industrial robot deployed in a warehouse. The talk will be in Room 206.
  • The ROI of Reality: Investing in the Physical AI Frontier: David Sokolic, a partner at Toyota Ventures, will break down what it takes to build, fund, and scale intelligent physical systems. The presentation will be in Room 207.
  • How to Pick Winners in Robotics: What Programs and IP to Pursue and Why: Spencer Krause, the president and CEO of SKA Robotics, go through some of the methodologies that Krause uses when evaluating the viability of a business case for robotics and also whether or not to accept a partner engagement. It will be in Room 209/210.
  • Intelligence Behind Warehouse Robotics: Scaling Operations with AI & Software: Jingwei Tan, a senior system consultant at Geek+, and Joe Kraft, the director of system consulting at Geek+, will examine how software, not just hardware, enables organizations to expand from a single automated workflow to enterprise-scale warehouse operations, while reducing complexity, improving resource utilization, and accelerating ROI. This RoboBusiness 2026 talk will take place in Room 204.
Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Reservoir opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship innovation hub. | Source: Reservoir

Reservoir, Washington State University’s Prosser Irrigated Agriculture Research and Extension Center (IAREC), the Washington Tree Fruit Research Commission (WTFRC), and the Tri-City Development Council (TRIDEC) today announced a new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers. 

The site will put agricultural robotics startups to work in the state’s orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers.

The announcement comes as Washington growers face rising labor costs and a shrinking workforce for some of the hardest crops in the world to automate. These include apples, cherries, pears, blueberries, wine grapes, and hops.

Reservoir is an agricultural innovation center and venture capital fund. The organization is focused on helping agtech startups succeed where agriculture happens, in the field.

Reservoir started its innovation center in the Salinas Valley. It hopes to expand to other key regions across California and the American West. Reservoir VC backs startups solving real problems in high-value crops and the rugged physical AI stack.

More about Reservoir’s innovation center

Earlier this year, the company officially opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship on-farm innovation hub for specialty crops. The new site features multiple innovation barns and 24 acres of dedicated commercial test fields. This creates the most concentrated ecosystem of technology leaders, growers, and startups anywhere in agriculture to rapidly scale solutions for global food production challenges.

More than 300 growers, agricultural leaders, federal and state officials, community partners, investors and media attended the grand opening of Salinas site.

“From our early days, Reservoir listened intently to partners to understand where innovation in agriculture was stuck,” said Danny Bernstein, founder and CEO of Reservoir. “Once our vision to create an on-farm innovation center was clear, we worked relentlessly with partners across the industry to bring the energy, focus and skills necessary to manifest the space and people necessary to make this a reality. With the doors open, the focus turns to execution and impact – in the form of real-world solutions for growers, upskilled jobs for rural communities, and a more secure food supply for American consumers.”

Last summer, Reservoir announced plans to expand its on-farm innovation center model across California, Arizona, and other major growing regions. Each hub will be anchored by leading academic and research and developmnt institutions.

As part of this multi-region strategy, Reservoir invited startups to run pilots over the winter months at the University of Arizona’s Yuma Agricultural Center. The startups gained the opportunity to test technologies in commercial desert vegetable production.

In August, Reservoir announced a $10 million, three-year R&D partnership with John Deere. The partnership aims to accelerate real-world development and commercialization of rugged AI technologies for high-value crop agriculture. It builds on a relationship that began when Reservoir was founded in 2024.

Deere said the partnership with Reservoir reflects its “commitment to an innovation ecosystem that moves faster from prototype to grower impact.”

Arrowfly, an award-winning B2B media and marketing company, today announced that RoboBusiness, the leading robotics industry event for the past 20 years, is being rebranded as Robotics Summit & Expo West, a conference and expo dedicated to the design, deployment, and scaling of commercial robots and businesses. The first event under the new name will be in October 2027 in Santa Clara, Calif.

The timing reflects how the industry has matured. Many robotics companies have moved past the prototype stage, shipping real products into factories, warehouses, and other sites. The questions that define their work are no longer only technical. They are about design for manufacturing, bringing products to market, implementation, managing growing fleets, and providing service and support. Robotics Summit & Expo West will help industry professionals meet increasing demand for intelligent systems across sectors.

“The robotics industry has matured, and the hardest problems have grown with it,” said Steve Crowe, executive editor of The Robot Report and chair of the Robotics Summit. “For 20 years, RoboBusiness brought this community together. Robotics Summit & Expo West will serve that community by sharing lessons from industry leaders on how to move from a pilot that works to a product deployed across multiple sites and building a business that can support it.”

Robotics Summit & Expo West is organized around the questions that define the post-prototype stage of a robotics company:

Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments.

Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services.

Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment.

Investment and growth: How investors evaluate robotics companies, and how founding teams can build businesses that last.

The conference program includes keynotes with industry and thought leaders, sessions focused on the latest technical and business topics, insightful panel discussions, and a curated expo floor. Attendees can learn from the founders, operators, and investors who are shaping the future of robotics.

One mission. Two conversations

The rebrand clarifies Arrowfly’s robotics event portfolio. Robotics Summit & Expo Boston (June 2–3, 2027, John B. Hynes Convention Center), the flagship East Coast show, focuses on the core technical and engineering challenges of building robotic systems. Robotics Summit & Expo West focuses on scaling the product and the company behind it. Together, the two events serve the full lifecycle of designing, building, and bringing a robotics product to market.

“Deployment does not end the development process. It changes who is asking the questions,” said Amanda Buehner, senior vice president of sales & strategy, engineering, at Arrowfly. “The engineer designing a new mobile robot and the operations leader managing robots across a warehouse network are both essential to this industry. They need different conversations. That is what the Robotics Summit lineup now provides.”

Robotics hardware, software, and solution providers looking to reach the engineers, product leaders, and executives scaling robotics can learn about sponsorship and exhibit opportunities by contacting Arrowfly’s robotics team.

About Arrowfly

Arrowfly is a live and digital B2B destination serving professionals across the engineering, healthcare, food, retail, and hospitality sectors. Across 40+ brands, the company delivers trusted journalism, original content, live and digital events, video, and demand generation programs to the decisionmakers shaping their industries. Powered by Clara, Arrowfly’s proprietary performance platform, partners get real-time visibility into audience engagement, lead quality, and campaign ROI. The company is backed by an established reputation for editorial independence and credibility across the markets it serves. For more information, visit arrowfly.com.

Aaron Parness, director of applied sciences at Amazon Robotics, and Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, speaking at the 2026 RBR50 gala.

The Robot Report is seeking nominations for its 2026 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards. The RBR50 has recognized the most innovative organizations and robots since 2012, and this year we’re rebranding to The Robot Report 50 (TRR50). Here are the winners from 2026, 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, and 2021.

Each year, The Robot Report selects the most interesting and important robotics innovations from around the world. The deadline for submissions is Friday, Jan. 5, 2027. Submit your nomination(s) below.

The TRR50 winners will be celebrated at an awards gala during the Robotics Summit & Expo, which will be held on June 2 and 3, 2027 in Boston. Some of the winners will also be demoing their robots on the Robotics Summit expo floor in the TRR50 Pavilion.

TRR50 Awards categories

To be eligible, all nominations must be for innovations that were initiated, released, or executed between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2026. The TRR50 is looking for submissions in the following categories:

Startup of the Year: The nominee must be less than five years, and it must be already testing its innovation with customers. Last year, Physical Intelligence, which offers AI models that change how robots learn, earned the Startup of the Year award, and the year before, Mytra took home the honors.

Application of the Year: The winner will be a use case that has previously been difficult to automate and where robotics and automation have demonstrated a clear benefit over previous processes. Last year, Harvard University won for its wearable robot aids to help those struggling after a stroke or with ALS. The year before, TEPCO won for its work to remove radioactive fuel from Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant.

Robot of the Year: The TRR50 awards are seeking a robot that is a game-changer in terms of technology innovation, use case, and industry influence. Amazon’s Vulcan robot won the award in 2026, and Robotaxi developer Waymo won in 2025.

Robots for Good: The TRR50 Robots for Good Award honors a robot that make a positive impact on society by addressing social challenges, improving quality of life or work, or promoting sustainability. Tatum Robotics won in 2026 for its robotic hand that enables tactile sign language communication. In 2025, Hello Robot’s Stretch 3 mobile manipulator won the inaugural Robots for Good Award.

Best use of AI: The TRR50 Best Use of AI Award will honor a real-world application for AI in robotics. This new category will highlight one use case that exemplifies how AI is changing robotics.

Products: This category honors new robots, enabling technologies, and research.

Komodo scans through deck coating without stripping them

Central to the expansion is Komodo, a proprietary Gecko robotic technology system. Komodo scans through thick, non-skid deck coatings without stripping or damaging them, giving the Navy the ability to see the health of assets without taking it apart.

It produces a full-deck heatmap of corrosion and material thickness, enabling repair teams to pinpoint damage and plan work before a ship enters drydock, which was previously possible only after maintenance had begun.

The ceiling increase comes as the Department of the Navy places greater emphasis on fleet readiness as a national security priority. Gecko’s wall-climbing robots, drones, and fixed-sensors collect an unprecedented amount of data on the health of U.S. Navy ships and submarines, including components, hulls, decks and welds, with AI being used to create accurate models to identify any current and future structural issues, even ones that cannot be seen by the human eye.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. 

Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. 

Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. 

“By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report. “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” 

That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems.

Building a pipeline for tactile data

Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed.

Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. 

The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. 

“Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. 

Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. 

The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. 

Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. 

“Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.”

That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications

Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. 

A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. 

The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. 

Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations.

The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. 

The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. 

Moving beyond visual perception

Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. 

Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. 

Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. 

Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. 

The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. 

But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. 

Scaling touch for robotics

The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. 

Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. 

Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. 

Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. 

Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. 

“The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.”
He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. 

For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks.

There are several factors to choosing brushless DC or BLDC motors for robots. Source: Faisal Mahmood

Selecting a brushless DC, or BLDC, motor for robotic arms or mobile robots starts with the mechanical system, not the controller catalog. A motor rated for a particular voltage and wattage does not tell an engineer whether it can deliver the required torque at low speed, regulate position accurately, absorb regenerative energy, or survive the thermal duty cycle.

The actuator is a system. The motor, inverter, current sensors, rotor position feedback, gearbox, brake, output encoder, thermal path, communications interface, and higher level robot software all influence the result.

An industrial or collaborative robotic arm joint generally prioritizes controllable torque, low-speed smoothness, position accuracy, collision response, backdrivability, and thermal performance. A mobile robot drive motor generally puts more emphasis on efficiency, starting torque, braking, traction, battery utilization, speed regulation, and synchronization between drive channels.

The terminology also deserves care. Commercial robotics literature often uses “BLDC” and “PMSM” (permanent magnet synchronous motor) somewhat interchangeably because both are three-phase, permanent-magnet machines driven by electronic inverters. Their back EMF waveform, winding design, controller algorithm, and feedback method still determine how a particular motor behaves.

For example, STMicroelectromics treats three-phase BLDC and PMSM control as related application areas and describes both six-step and field-oriented control architectures.

Start with the mechanical load, not the controller catalog

The first selection exercise is to establish what the motor actually has to do. For a geared robotic joint, a useful first order relationship is: τ_joint = (τ_motor × gear ratio × η_gear) − τ_losses

Motor speed follows the transmission ratio: ω_motor = ω_joint × gear ratio

Mechanical power is: P_mech = τ × ω

And a first approximation of battery side electrical power is: P_elec ≈ P_mech / η_total

These equations do not replace a dynamic model, but they expose the parameters that matter before a controller is selected. Considerations include continuous torque, peak torque, peak duration, acceleration torque, gravity torque, and reflected inertia. In addition, regenerative braking, stall or near stall operation, duty cycle, thermal resistance, battery voltage range, and cable and connector current limits should all be established.

For robotic arms, the load calculation has to account for link inertia, payload, gravity compensation, gearbox ratio, backlash, compliance, counterbalance, and encoder location. A motor side encoder can report the rotor position accurately while the joint output still contains transmission error.

For mobile robots, the equivalent exercise starts with vehicle mass, wheel radius, rolling resistance, slope, acceleration, terrain, wheel slip, and drive configuration. Differential-drive platforms impose different synchronization requirements from four wheel drive vehicles. An outdoor uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) can also spend much more time in high load operation than a lightweight indoor delivery robot.

Regenerative energy deserves particular attention. During deceleration or downhill travel, the motor can return energy to the DC bus. The battery, controller, braking strategy, and bus capacitance all have to accommodate that energy. A controller that handles acceleration correctly can still create an over-voltage problem during aggressive regenerative braking.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Choose the commutation method according to motion quality

Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior.

Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations.

Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning.

Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components.

The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM).

In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM.

FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications.

FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error.

Select the feedback architecture

Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems.

Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information.

Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence.

Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important.

The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position.

That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase.

Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy.

Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate.

Match the controller to the robotic arm

A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback.

A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control.

This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task.

An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller.

The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier.

The Robot Report‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components.

For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function.

Match the controller to the mobile robot

BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment.

A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide.

Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods of sustained power.

Battery behavior also changes the controller decision. Voltage sag under acceleration reduces the available electrical headroom, while regenerative braking can raise DC bus voltage. A controller designed around a nominal battery voltage therefore needs to be evaluated over the complete battery operating range rather than at one nominal value.

Thermal design is another difference. A drive enclosed inside a wheel or compact chassis may have limited airflow. The inverter, motor windings, bearings, connectors, and mechanical structure all become part of the heat path.

Harmonic Drive‘s servo-grade propulsion drive trains for AMRs illustrate this system-level relationship. Their characteristics include smooth travel, backdrivability, torque density, stiffness, and radial load support. The lesson is not that one transmission is appropriate for every AMR, but that propulsion control cannot be separated from the drivetrain.

Mobile manipulators make the distinction even more obvious. Desmasa’s MCR+ combined a robot arm and an AMR that shared one power and control architecture. The drive requirements of the base remained different from those of the arm, even though both ultimately contained electric actuators.

Evaluate current sensing and thermal behavior

Controller current ratings require careful interpretation. A datasheet may list continuous phase current, continuous bus current, peak phase current, peak current duration, RMS current, or a configurable current limit. These numbers are not interchangeable.

The motor’s thermal limit, inverter semiconductor limit, connector rating, cable rating, and battery capability can all be lower than a headline peak current specification. A controller advertised with a large peak current is therefore not automatically suitable for a motor that requires that current continuously.

BLDC.com provides a useful commercial example of the specification categories engineers encounter in controller selection. Its current controller catalog lists different input voltage ranges and current ratings across several controller families, while individual products describe interfaces and protection features.

Those specifications illustrate why engineers should compare voltage range, current definition, duration, feedback compatibility, and protection functions rather than simply comparing wattage.

The heat path must also be considered. Motor winding losses have to leave the motor through its structure and mounting arrangement. Power stage losses must leave the inverter through its enclosure, thermal interface, heat sink, airflow, or mounting structure. Thermal testing under the actual duty cycle is more informative than relying only on a short unloaded bench test.

Consider the communications and software layers

The motor controller is normally responsible for the fastest control loops. A robot controller does not need to calculate every PWM transition. Instead, the drive can execute current regulation and commutation locally while receiving higher level torque, velocity, or position commands.

Before selecting a drive, engineers should check CAN or CANopen support, EtherCAT support, RS 485 or UART, analog and PWM inputs, encoder interfaces, feedback update rates, command latency, fault reporting, firmware update procedures, parameter storage, multi axis synchronization, ROS 2 or ros2_control integration, and CiA 402 support where applicable.

CANopen’s CiA 402 profile standardizes functional behavior for servo drives and other motion control devices, including operating states and command/status structures. That can simplify interoperability when the selected hardware actually implements the required profile.

EtherCAT becomes attractive when synchronized multi axis motion and deterministic timing are central requirements. Its distributed clock architecture allows participating devices to synchronize their local timing.

ROS 2 integration is a separate consideration from the physical bus. Ros2_control represents robot hardware through command and state interfaces and provides a framework for connecting controllers to physical actuators. The controller manager also emphasizes deterministic control loop execution, showing why communication availability alone does not guarantee real time behavior.

Treat safety as an architecture, not a checkbox

A motor controller should be evaluated for overcurrent, short circuit, overvoltage, undervoltage, overtemperature, overspeed, encoder failure, Hall failure, phase loss, stall detection, brake control, communications loss, regenerative voltage rise, unintended restart, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque off where applicable.

These functions are not automatically equivalent to a complete safety architecture. Safety requirements depend on the robot category, risk assessment, operating environment, and system design.

For industrial robots, ISO 10218 1:2025 specifies safety requirements for industrial robots. ISO 13849 1:2023 addresses the design of safety related parts of control systems, including software. IEC 61800 5 2 addresses functional safety considerations for safety related adjustable speed power drive systems.

The important engineering distinction is that a controller having an overcurrent shutdown or temperature sensor does not, by itself, establish a certified safety function. The safety function has to be designed, validated, and integrated according to the applicable requirements.

A practical selection workflow

A useful motor controller selection process can be reduced to ten engineering steps.

  • Step 1: Define the complete load and motion profile, including acceleration, deceleration, payload, terrain, gravity, and duty cycle.
  • Step 2: Calculate continuous and peak torque at the motor shaft and, where applicable, at the joint or wheel.
  • Step 3: Establish the required speed, acceleration, operating range, and regenerative braking conditions.
  • Step 4: Define the control objective: speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction.
  • Step 5: Select feedback according to the actual control objective and mechanical transmission.
  • Step 6: Select six step, sinusoidal, or FOC control based on motion quality, speed range, torque requirements, and implementation constraints.
  • Step 7: Check voltage, continuous and peak current, regeneration, thermal margins, and battery behavior.
  • Step 8: Select the communication and software interfaces needed by the robot architecture.
  • Step 9: Define safety behavior, fault response, braking, communication loss behavior, and restart conditions.
  • Step 10: Validate the complete motor, drive, gearbox, sensor, brake, and robot controller as one system.

BLDC motor control selection decision table

Application requirement Preferred control direction Main reason Important limitation
Simple wheel speed control Sensored six step or simple closed loop control Low implementation complexity Coarser torque and position behavior
High-efficiency mobile traction FOC with appropriate feedback Good torque and speed regulation across a wide operating range Higher software and tuning complexity
Low-speed robotic joint motion Encoder based FOC Smooth torque production and precise rotor angle information Transmission and tuning still limit performance
High precision joint positioning Servo drive with encoder feedback, potentially output feedback Position loop can account for joint behavior More sensors, wiring, and integration effort
Torque controlled collaborative joint FOC servo architecture with suitable torque feedback or estimation Fast current/torque response Safety and torque accuracy require system validation
Sensorless high speed drive Sensorless commutation or sensorless FOC Eliminates position sensors and wiring Startup and very low speed behavior require careful design
Multi axis synchronized arm Networked servo drives, often with deterministic Ethernet Coordinated timing and distributed control Network and drive configuration become part of commissioning
Harsh outdoor mobile robot Closed loop drive with feedback selected for the environment Better speed control, diagnostics, and traction management Environmental sealing and thermal design remain system level issues

Commissioning and validation

A controller should not move directly from a wiring diagram to production operation. First, verify phase order and encoder direction. Confirm Hall or encoder alignment and current sense polarity. Run the motor unloaded at reduced voltage where the hardware permits it, then compare commanded and measured speed.

Next, check position error and current behavior. Apply a controlled mechanical load and measure phase current and bus current. Monitor motor and inverter temperatures during acceleration, steady operation, and repeated cycles.

Regenerative braking deserves a dedicated test. Measure the DC bus during controlled deceleration and confirm that the battery, braking circuit, and controller remain within their operating limits.

Communication loss testing should verify what the drive actually does when commands stop arriving. Sensor disconnection tests should confirm fault detection and the resulting state. Overcurrent, thermal protection, emergency stop, and brake behavior should also be tested under controlled conditions.

Finally, repeat the important tests after thermal soak. A drive that behaves correctly for several minutes at room temperature may behave differently after the motor and inverter reach their operating temperatures.

For a robotic arm, these tests should be performed with the gearbox and representative mechanism installed. For a mobile robot, they should include the actual wheel, vehicle mass, battery, terrain, and representative duty cycle. A bench test of an unloaded motor validates only part of the system.

Engineer’s checklist

  1. What are the continuous and peak torque requirements?
  2. What is the required speed and acceleration range?
  3. Is the objective speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction control?
  4. Is Hall feedback sufficient, or is encoder feedback required?
  5. Is motor side feedback sufficient for the mechanical transmission?
  6. Does six step control provide adequate motion quality, or is FOC justified?
  7. Are voltage, current, regeneration, and thermal margins adequate?
  8. Does the communications interface meet latency and synchronization requirements?
  9. What happens during sensor failure, communication loss, braking, and emergency stop?
  10. Has the complete actuator been tested under the actual mechanical duty cycle?

Pulling together criteria to pick the right motor

The correct BLDC motor control architecture is determined by the control variable, mechanical transmission, feedback quality, duty cycle, thermal limits, energy system, safety architecture, and software integration.

For a simple mobile drive, a sensored six-step controller may provide an adequate combination of cost, robustness, and speed regulation. A demanding robotic joint may instead require encoder based FOC, nested torque, velocity, and position loops, and possibly output side feedback.

An outdoor mobile platform may need closed loop traction control, careful regenerative energy management, environmental protection, and thermal capacity that would be unnecessary on a small indoor robot.

The key decision is therefore not simply which BLDC motor controller has the right voltage or wattage rating. The useful question is whether the complete motor, inverter, feedback system, transmission, power source, communications layer, and safety architecture can produce the required behavior throughout the robot’s actual operating envelope.

The Report Report presents a whitepaper on the race to physical AI.

AI has become remarkably good at understanding language, images, and code. The next challenge is harder — understanding reality, according to Analog Devices Inc. or ADI. Physical AI moves intelligence out of digital environments and into machines that must sense, decide, and act in the world.

Unlike software, those systems face imperfect measurements, timing constraints, changing conditions, and the consequences of action, said the company in a new report.
