The post The rise of the machines is canceled: Why humanoids with AI are helpers, not enemies appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid, shown here, is an example of a robot ready for AI.

For decades, engineers have been trying to create robots that look and act like humans. Now, rapid advances in artificial intelligence are bringing humanoid robots out of the lab and onto the factory floor. As fears grow that AI will displace workers, a global race is underway to develop humanoid robots capable of performing human work.

Competitors include Tesla, startups backed by Amazon and NVIDIA, and state-owned Chinese companies. Waltham, Mass.-based Boston Dynamics, valued at over $1 billion, is among the humanoid leaders with its Atlas robot. South Korean automaker Hyundai owns an 88% stake in the company.

Hyundai‘s massive auto plant is arguably the most advanced in the world. More than 1,000 robots work alongside nearly 1,500 humans, lifting, stamping, and welding parts in robotic unison. Atlas, at 175 cm (68.8 in.) tall and 90 kg (198.4 lb.) in weight, has left the lab and is doing real work.

Atlas and AI learn with human help

Atlas’s development is led by Zach Jackowski. He holds two degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT, and his mission is to transform the robot into a productive worker on the factory floor. Atlas confidently helps sort roof racks for the assembly line without human intervention. It operates autonomously; many roboticists would have considered this insane five or six years ago.

In 2021, Atlas was a bulky, hydraulic robot that could only run and jump. Back then, Atlas relied on algorithms written by engineers. The next-generation Atlas, with its sleek, all-electric body and AI, runs on cutting-edge NVIDIA chips, making it intelligent enough to autonomously perform incredible stunts.

Scott Kindersma led robotics research department at Boston Dynamics before moving to Google DeepMind. He explained that modern robots have learned to master movements that until recently were considered too complex for a machine. This is largely due to how these robots are programmed: more emphasis is placed on demonstrations and machine learning than on manual programming.

This humanoid can learn. Atlas learns in a variety of ways. In supervised training, machine learning specialist Kevin Bergerman (now also at Google DeepMind), wearing a virtual reality headset, took direct control of the humanoid, guiding its hand and arm movements step by step through each task until Atlas masters it. If this teleoperator can perform the task we want the robot to perform, this generates data that is subsequently used to train the robot’s AI models to perform that task autonomously.

The stylish suit you wear will actually record all your body movements to train Atlas to accurately mimic your movements. In this way, you will serve as a physical prototype for a 200-lb. metal robot. All your movements—walking, hand gestures—are captured by these sensors.

Engineers then feed this data into a machine learning process. Atlas’s body is different from yours, so they had to teach it to virtually imitate human movements. Over 4,000 digital Atlases were trained for six hours in a simulation. The simulation added complex challenges for the avatars, such as slippery floors, bending, and stiff joints.

Ultimately, this could lead to many copies of Atlas, each having loaded new skills into the AI ​​system. Once one robot is trained, they are all trained. Using the same processes, Atlas was taught to crawl and cartwheel. It wasn’t as good at duck walking.

Indeed, Atlas, or any other humanoid, can’t yet do most of the things a person does in their daily lives. For example, simply getting dressed in the morning or pouring a cup of coffee and carrying it around the house are too complex for Atlas.

What particularly stands out about Atlas is its brain. NVIDIA chips—the same ones that helped launch the AI ​​revolution with GPT chat—process a stream of collected data, bringing this humanoid robot closer to a semblance of common sense. Atlas can see its surroundings and understands how the physical world works.

One day, you’ll be able to place such a robot in a factory and simply explain to it what you want it to do. It will have enough knowledge of how the world works to perform the tasks assigned to it.

Spot platform demonstrates legged robot utility

There’s currently a lot of excitement in the industry about the potential of creating robots smart enough to be truly versatile. Robert Playter, CEO of Boston Dynamics, led the company’s robotics development until stepping down earlier this year.

The cornerstone was the robotic dog Spot, introduced almost 10 years ago. The quadruped is trained to work in hot, cold, and rugged conditions, roaming the halls of Boston Dynamics.

It has multiple cameras, thermal sensors, acoustic sensors, and an array of sensors on its back that allow it to collect data on the plant’s condition. Spot conducts quality checks at the Hyundai plant, ensuring that cars are equipped with the necessary parts. They conduct safety checks and industrial inspections at hundreds of facilities around the world. What began with Spot has evolved into Atlas. This robot is capable of superhuman movement.

Therefore, it will be able to surpass what we can do. “So, you’re creating a robot that should surpass human capabilities.”

“Why not, right? We’d love to invent creatures that could be stronger than us, withstand higher temperatures than us, or enter dangerous places.” Superhuman capabilities—for many people, that sounds terrifying. You’re not envisioning a Terminator world.

Absolutely not. If you saw how hard it takes to get robots to perform some of the simple tasks required of them, it would allay fears about intelligent and out-of-control machines. Could people have more pressing concerns?

It’s guaranteed that there will be people who say, “I’ll lose my job to a robot.” Work is truly changing. So monotonous, grueling work will eventually be performed by robots.

But these robots aren’t so autonomous that they don’t need to be managed. They need to be built, trained, and maintained. It could be several years before Atlas joins the Hyundai team permanently. Goldman Sachs predicts the humanoid robot market will reach $38 billion within a decade.

The humanoid robot race continues

Boston Dynamics and other U.S. robot makers are vying for the lead, but they’re not alone in the competition. Chinese companies are proving themselves to be formidable competitors. They’re determined to win.

Are they ahead of us?

The Chinese government is on a mission: to win the robotics race. Technically, we’re still ahead, but there’s a real risk that, simply due to the scale of our investments, we could fall behind.

To stay ahead, Hyundai has made a major investment in Boston Dynamics. This is the beginning of a long journey. The ultimate goal is the human-like future we mentioned at the beginning. Robots like us, working alongside us, walking among us.

Editor’s note: Physical AI and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

AI moves toward superhuman capabilities

When Demis Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in 2024, he celebrated by playing poker with the world chess champion. Hassabis loves games, which is how he became an artificial intelligence pioneer. The British scientist is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind.

A few years ago, chatbots heralded a new era. Now, Hassabis and others are striving to create what’s known as artificial general intelligence—a silicon-based intelligence as versatile as a human, but with superhuman speed and knowledge.

“I’ve always been driven and intrigued by understanding the world around us,” said Hassabis. “Since childhood, I’ve been fascinated by big questions: the meaning of life, the nature of consciousness, the nature of reality itself.”

“I loved reading about the great scientists and philosophers who worked on these problems, and I wanted to see if we could advance human knowledge,” he recalled. “For me, the expression of this desire has been the creation of what I consider the perfect tool for advancing human knowledge: artificial intelligence.”

Hassabis noted that AI is advancing quickly, attracting attention, resources, and talent. Early chatbots only explored the internet. An app called Astra perceives the world. It was able to make up stories after being shown paintings. But such systems are still learning about context and may develop unexpected skills.

“So, new capabilities or properties may emerge as a result of learning. This may worry people,” Hassabis acknowledged. “The duality of these types of systems is that they are capable of incredible things, going beyond what we can design or understand ourselves.”

From AGI to robotics

As AI begins to take on tasks such as booking flights and shopping online, it is taking steps toward AGI. By 2030, we could have systems that truly understand their surroundings and are integrated into our daily lives. This is where robots come in.

Once a robot can perceive, understand, decide, and act, it can begin to do truly useful things. Researchers Alex Lee and Julia Vassallo have demonstrated a robot that understands what it sees. It’s not easy. And it reasons by following vague instructions. “Place the blocks whose colors correspond to the combination of yellow and blue into the corresponding ball.” The combination of yellow and blue is green. And the robot figured it out.

Is Hassabis working on a system that would be self-aware?

“I don’t think any modern system feels self-aware or, you know, conscious in any sense,” he replied. “Obviously, everyone needs to make their own decisions when interacting with these chatbots. I think it’s theoretically possible. But is self-awareness your goal? It might happen implicitly. These systems might acquire some sense of self-awareness. It’s important for these systems to understand you, themselves, and others, and that’s the beginning of self-awareness.”

“If a machine becomes self-aware, we might not recognize it,” continued Hassabis. “There are two reasons why we consider each other conscious. One is that you exhibit the behavior of a conscious being. The second is that you operate on the same foundation. We are made of the same carbon material, and our brains are soft and flexible. Machines operate on silicon. So, even if they exhibit the same behavior and say the same things, that doesn’t necessarily mean the sense of consciousness we experience is the same as theirs.”

Hassabis told us that AI could lead to what he called “radical abundance,” the elimination of scarcity. But he also gave a warning.

“There are two things that worry me. One is that malicious actors will repurpose these systems for harm,” said Hassabis. “The second question concerns the AI ​​systems themselves. As they become increasingly autonomous and powerful, can we ensure that we can control these systems, that they align with our values, that they do what we want, that they benefit society, and that they remain within established constraints?”

Can an AI agent be taught morality? “I think so,” Hassabis responded. “They learn by doing, by teaching others. And I think this is one of the challenges we must address: giving them a value system, guidance, and some constraints, just like we teach a child.”

Google DeepMind is competing with dozens of other companies striving to create AGI that you won’t be able to distinguish from human intelligence. It announced its Gemini 2 foundation model in August and Gemini 4 Argon this week.

Anduril founder says robots and AI can reduce risk

Some international groups call such weapons killer robots. But Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, said they represent the future of warfare—a working product that eliminates risks. Once a child prodigy, Luckey sold Oculus to Facebook for $2 billion.

He ultimately decided to move into the defense industry. The billionaire owns an autonomous speedboat called Dive XL. It is not remote-controlled, and Anduril claimed that it can travel 1,000 miles fully submerged. Australia has already invested $58 million in such submarines.

Tucked away inside a hangar is an Anduril unmanned fighter jet called the Fury. It has no cockpit, control stick, or rudder because there’s no pilot. Some in the defense industry viewed Anduril as just another tech startup until it beat out several leading defense contractors in the competition to build an unmanned fighter jet for the U.S. Air Force.

About the author

Elena Krosheva is a freelance journalist, marketing analyst, and SEO specialist. She graduated with honors from the Faculty of Journalism at the Institute of Modern Knowledge in Minsk, Belarus, in 2007.

Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.

]]> Legora, the Swedish agentic operating system for legal professionals, today announced it has raised a €489 million ($550 million) Series E at an €7.8 bilion ($8.8 billion) post-money valuation in order to continue its international expansion and double down on the Legora aOS.

The round was led by Atreides Management, with participation from new investors, including Baron Capital, Capital Research, Fidelity Management & Research Company, and Glade Brook Capital Partners. Every major existing investor, including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Insight Venture Partners, Redpoint Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, and Sands Capital, is also participating.

“The opportunity in legal is enormous and we are still early. AI is changing the role of the lawyer, with more time for judgement and advice, and it is reshaping how law firms and in-house legal teams are organised and how their work gets done. We intend to lead that shift in the US and globally. We chose investors who share our long-term view and know what it takes to build a lasting company. They are the right partners for the years ahead,” says Max Junestrand, CEO and co-founder of Legora.

Legora’s latest funding builds on a rapid expansion documented in our earlier coverage.

The Stockholm-based company raised €70.6 million in a Series B in May 2025 at a €596 million valuation, before a €42 million extension to its Series D in April 2026 brought that round to €513 million at a €4.7 billion valuation.

Its expansion has also involved acquisitions, including London-based Wexler, its fifth acquisition of 2026.

The new financing comes alongside other European legal AI investments this year, including €60.2 million for Edinburgh-based Wordsmith, €50 million each for London’s Orbital and Lawhive, €42.9 million for Milan-based Lexroom, and €13.5 million for Copenhagen-based Pandektes. In Sweden, Malmö-based Lightbringer secured €8.6 million for its AI-powered patent platform, while Stockholm’s Hybridity raised €2 million for regulatory compliance automation.

These and other 2026 rounds represent approximately €237.7 million in funding, rising to €726.7 million when Legora’s new Series E is included, illustrating the relative scale of its latest investment within this group of European legal and adjacent AI companies.

“Legal is a sophisticated market with demanding buyers, and the bar for software is high. Legora has become the platform that law firms and in-house legal teams adopt and then expand across their organisations, and it has done so while growing at remarkable speed. Legora has also built a sustainable business along the way, with the discipline to scale fast and stay efficient. We are excited to support the team as Legora enters its next stage of growth in the US and globally,” adds Gavin Baker, Managing Partner and CIO at Atreides.

Founded in 2023, Legora is the agentic operating system for legal work, supporting lawyers in research, review, and drafting across complex matters. It now has more than 1,000 employees across 18 offices and is used by more than 140,000 legal professionals at more than 2,400 leading law firms and in-house legal teams across over 80 markets.

The round follows a period of rapid growth for the unicorn. Legora went from $1 million to $100 million in ARR in less than 18 months, allegedly faster than any other enterprise software company selling through a direct sales team, and the next $100 million took less than six months. ARR now stands at more than €178 million ($200 million). The new valuation compares with €4.9 billion ($5.6 billion) at the company’s previous round.

In-house legal teams, only a small fraction of Legora’s customer base a year ago, made up more than 40% of new customers in the third quarter. In the United States, now Legora’s largest market by revenue, more than half of the AmLaw 50 are customers, and Legora opened its first US office only in spring 2025.

The capital will support continued expansion in North America, where Legora has offices in New York, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Francisco, Toronto and Mexico City, as well as in its markets across Europe and Asia-Pacific.

It will also deepen investment in the Legora aOS, the agentic operating system that lawyers and their agents work in; bringing new products like agentic in-take, horizon scanning and legal research to life.

“Growth only counts if the business underneath it holds up. We have passed $200 million in ARR, and we want every dollar of it to be a durable one. That means healthy gross margins, high retention, and a cost structure that gets stronger as we scale. This round lets us keep building that way,” says David Eckstein, CFO at Legora.

]]> Fuse Energy, a British energy company, has opened reservations for Fuse Compute, its first commercial AI product, offering access to NVIDIA GPUs in UK data centres powered by Fuse – marking a new step into AI infrastructure by the EnergyTech startup.

Interested parties can register interest and reserve capacity today, with the first GPUs slated to come online in December 2026. The ambition here is to own the full AI stack: power, land, data centres and AI compute.

“Power is the biggest hurdle to building AI infrastructure, and it’s the part we already know how to do,” says Alan Chang, CEO and co-founder of Fuse Energy. “Every AI company is fighting for the same scarce GPUs, and the grid can’t connect data centres fast enough to keep up. Fuse Compute puts that expertise to work for the companies building the future of intelligence, and makes sure that future is built in Britain.”

This is an interesting new direction for an energy company whose focus is simplyfying gas and electricity management. Fuse has raised €178 million ($199 million) since its founding in 2022.

Our earlier coverage traces Fuse’s expansion from supplying 50,000 UK homes in July 2025, when it reported €76 million in annualised revenue and raised €8.5 million, to more than 200,000 households and €341 million in annual recurring revenue by December, when it secured another €59 million.

By June 2026, Fuse was supplying more than 300,000 households and had closed a €25 million Series B extension, while reporting monthly EBITDA profitability since December 2025.

Its expansion into AI compute comes amid significant funding for companies developing the underlying infrastructure. In the UK, Nscale raised €1.7 billion for vertically integrated AI compute, Volta reportedly secured €259.8 million across two rounds to develop AI factories, and Orbital Industries raised €43 million for industrial hardware including data-centre technologies.

Elsewhere, Finland’s Verda raised €164.8 million for AI cloud expansion and Spain’s iPronics secured €107.6 million for optical networking. These 2026 infrastructure financing announcements totalled approximately €2.4 billion, excluding Fuse’s historical funding.

The company says that AI is creating more demand for compute than the UK can supply. The UK Government’s Compute Roadmap estimates the country will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030, yet new data centres face waits of up to a decade for a grid connection.

Power has become the main constraint on how quickly that capacity can be built. The Government aims to expand the UK’s public compute capacity 20x by 2030, but the country has few home-grown providers of large-scale compute, leaving many British AI companies reliant on capacity hosted overseas.

Fuse’s move into compute builds on its experience in power. Its most recent solar site was built at around 30% below the industry average cost per megawatt. It holds a power generation pipeline of more than 1GW and a data centre connection pipeline of 142MW across 15 projects. This will allow it to energise and construct high-density AI sites quickly and cheaply.

Fuse Compute will offer bare-metal, single-tenant NVIDIA GPU nodes in UK data centres, with UK jurisdiction and a UK data path. The first 128 NVIDIA B300 GPUs are due to come online in December 2026, followed by 1,024 in Q2 2027, a further 22MW in Q4 2027 and 116MW from 2028.

In energy, Fuse already supplies 470,000 UK homes and holds both supplier and meter operator licences.

On the supply side, Fuse owns and operates low carbon generation assets, with 22 MW active and over 1 GW in the pipeline across the UK, US, and Europe.

For the company, keeping compute onshore means that the data will stay under UK jurisdiction, and that British AI companies will no longer need to rely on overseas capacity.

Fuse’s near-term data centre projects will also reportedly bring 250 construction and operational jobs to the UK, and represent €1.1 billion (£1 billion) of investment in UK infrastructure.

]]> Photon Bridge (formerly Photon IP), an Eindhoven-based startup building optical engines for AI and telecom, has raised €10 million to tackle an emerging bottleneck in AI infrastructure: producing the millions of lasers needed to connect increasingly large clusters of AI processors.

New investors, the Amadeus APEX Technology Fund and 360 Capital, co-led the round, while existing investors Innovation Industries, Faber, and Brabant Development Agency (BOM) also increased their investment. In January 2025, the company announced it had secured a €4.75 million Seed round led by Innovation Industries. 

“Every new wave of compute creates new bottlenecks further down the supply chain, and lasers are the next one. Photon Bridge is addressing this with a technology that combines deep photonics expertise with a credible path towards manufacturing at very large scale,” said Ion Hauer, Investment Partner at APEX Ventures. 

Photon Bridge was founded in 2020 in Eindhoven by Rui Santos and Xaveer Leijtens to rethink how high-performance photonic systems are built at scale. The company says it is building laser sources for a market expected to need millions of units as optical connections move closer to AI chips.

It develops high-power, multi-wavelength laser-source technology for next-generation optical interconnects in AI data centres.

According to the startup, data transfer between processors is becoming a performance constraint as AI clusters expand from thousands to hundreds of thousands of chips. It notes that optical connections can move enormous amounts of data faster and more efficiently than conventional electrical interconnects, prompting their integration closer to processors. 

It also notes that this shift is accelerating with the emergence of co-packaged optics, which integrates optical connectivity directly alongside the chips that move data through AI systems. The startup says that this, in turn, drives demand for the lasers that supply light to these connections.

“Today’s high-power laser supply chain was largely built for telecom and subsea networks, where volumes are far lower. AI could transform the laser from a specialist photonics component into something that has to be manufactured at semiconductor scale. Photon Bridge has designed its technology around that transition,” the company mentioned in the press release 

Rather than generating the required optical power using a small number of increasingly powerful lasers, Photon Bridge claims that it combines and multiplexes light from multiple lower-power semiconductor lasers.

The Dutch startup says this approach reduces power densities, making individual lasers less sensitive to manufacturing defects, improving production yield and allowing Photon Bridge’s architecture to scale more efficiently as volumes increase.

The platform is designed to deliver high wavelength counts with up to 40 mW of optical power per wavelength per fibre, while enabling production across multiple indium phosphide (InP) foundries.

In September 2025, Photon IP rebranded as Photon Bridge and appointed Paul Marchal as CEO.

Marchal, CEO of Photon Bridge, said, “AI is fundamentally changing the way computing infrastructure is built. We are moving towards enormous systems in which hundreds of thousands of processors have to operate together, and moving data between them is becoming one of the defining constraints on performance.

“That means optics has to move closer to the compute. But it also creates an entirely different manufacturing challenge. The industry will soon need millions of these laser sources every year. Instead of making individual lasers increasingly powerful and difficult to manufacture, we move that scaling challenge into the architecture.”

Photon Bridge highlights that its approach is designed around manufacturing yield, a consideration that becomes increasingly important as laser production shifts from traditional telecom volumes to the scale required by AI infrastructure.

“AI is turning lasers from a telecom component into a semiconductor-scale product. Once you start talking about millions of units a year, manufacturing yield becomes fundamental. Photon Bridge has designed its architecture from the beginning around the volumes this market is going to require,” said Cesare Maifredi, Partner at 360 Capital.

The company plans to use this capital to accelerate product development and customer qualification, deliver its first samples in 2027, and prepare for volume manufacturing from 2028. Photon Bridge will also expand its Eindhoven team as it moves toward commercialisation.

]]> Skyfly Technologies, a British developer of electric and hybrid-electric vertical take-off aircraft, has closed an €8.91 million ($10 million) Seed round.

The round was led by HICO Investment Group, a specialist growth equity investor, with participation from Archangel, a €50 million early-stage fund and Europe’s only dedicated next-generation defence technology venture fund.

“What Skyfly’s team has achieved with so little is remarkable: a new aircraft, designed and built from scratch, flying and now leading the way through a brand-new certification pathway. We’re excited to back a team with a big vision and relentless drive to execute,” said Chris Hartnoll, Managing Director, HICO Investment Group.

Founded in 2019 and based in Thorpe Mandeville, Oxfordshire, Skyfly develops manned and unmanned aircraft and systems for civilian and defence markets. Its flagship product, the Axe, is a two-seat, fully electric, vertically-capable aircraft with a range of more than 100 miles and a cruise speed of 100mph, requiring no runway for take-off or landing. The Longbow is its hybrid-electric unmanned derivative for defence and government customers. 

The Axe is developed under the leadership of CTO Dr. William Brooks, who has spent over three decades in light aircraft development and has certified more than 2,000 aircraft currently in service. Axe takes off like a helicopter using eight fixed-angle electric motors, transitions to forward flight where its wings generate aerodynamic lift and can operate from conventional runways.

Since there are no tilting motors or rotary wings, Axe is designed to eliminate the mechanical complexity and potential points of failure that characterise many eVTOL concepts. In an emergency power loss scenario, the winged design allows the aircraft to glide rather than fall. 

The Axe offers a range of over 100 miles, a flight time of 60 to 90 minutes, a cruising speed of 100mph and a 200kg payload capacity. Skyfly projects an operating cost of around €83.57 (£70) per flight, which gives it a favourable standing against the likes of legacy two-seater aircrafts such as Robinson R22 or Cessna 152.

Longbow, Skyfly’s second aircraft, is a hybrid-electric unmanned aircraft with a range exceeding 400 miles and the same 200kg payload. It is designed for cargo resupply, intelligence and surveillance, medevac, and ship-to-shore logistics missions. The company says both the aircraft will be manufactured at Skyfly’s 10,000 sq.ft. facility in Thorpe Mandeville, Oxfordshire.

“Longbow addresses a clear requirement for unmanned systems that can move meaningful payloads over significant distances without relying on a runway. Archangel invests exclusively in defence-first companies, and our backing of Skyfly reflects the potential we see in its technology to deliver mission necessary capability for the modern battlespace,” said Nicholas Nelson, General Partner at Archangel Ventures.

Skyfly says its Axe prototype has completed more than 100 piloted flights, including Europe’s first airfield-to-airfield eVTOL flight. It holds experimental flight permits in both the UK and the US, and sixty-one private customers globally have already placed orders. 

The fundraise comes amid a regulatory shift, with the FAA’s MOSAIC reforms taking effect in July 2026. The MOSAIC reforms rewrote the rules governing Light Sport Aircraft to admit electric propulsion, multi-motor architectures and vertical take-off aircraft into a category that has been historically restricted to private owners rather than commercial operators. Skyfly says its Axe, a two-seat electric Vertically Capable Aircraft (eVCA) classified as Light Sport-class, was designed precisely for this rulebook.

Michael Thompson, founder and CEO of Skyfly, said, “This investment gives us the resources to take the Axe from a flying prototype to a certified aircraft in customers’ hands. The FAA’s MOSAIC rules have opened a route to market that simply did not exist for electric aircraft before, and the Axe was designed for exactly this category. HICO and Archangel understood that timing, and their backing lets us move at the pace the opportunity demands: completing certification and standing up series production.”

The fresh capital will be deployed across three areas: completing FAA Light Sport Aircraft certification for the Axe under the MOSAIC rules, scaling manufacturing capacity on both sides of the Atlantic, and accelerating development of the Longbow.

The post The cash cost of a 60-day customer (Sponsored) appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> A bigger UK contract can consume runway before it creates cash. Put the payment terms into the funding plan before signing.

A large UK customer offers a scale-up a contract with 60-day payment terms. The revenue looks attractive. The less visible question is how much cash the startup must find before the customer pays.

Before signing, put the collection date into the cash forecast and compare it with when wages, suppliers and taxes must be paid. Then test what happens if payment takes longer. A profitable contract can still need funding, and a revenue target does not supply it.

This matters particularly for founders selling services or software to larger organizations. The customer may have enough money to pay. It may also have a procurement process that requires a purchase order, an approved invoice and a particular payment run. Winning the account and financing the account are different jobs.

Thirty more days can tie up nearly £400,000

Start with a simple illustration, not an actual company. Assume annual UK credit sales of £4.8 million, spread evenly through the year, with invoices issued as sales occur. Ignore VAT, seasonality, bad debt and other changes for now.

At 30 days from invoicing to cash, average receivables would be roughly £395,000. At 60 days, they would be about £789,000. The extra 30 days ties up approximately £395,000 in invoices, without adding a pound of annual revenue.

The calculation is annual credit sales divided by 365, multiplied by the extra days to payment. Here that is £4.8 million ÷ 365 × 30, or £394,521 rounded to the nearest pound. If only part of the customer base changes terms, use that part’s sales, not the whole company’s turnover.

This is an estimate of additional receivables, not a precise funding requirement. Cash already held, supplier terms, deposits and the timing of delivery costs affect the amount the company must finance. Fast growth can also make a steady annual average misleading. Model the actual expected invoices and receipts month by month before deciding how much liquidity is needed.

The distinction is important: the £395,000 has not necessarily been lost. It is unavailable for payroll or the next product release while the business waits. The British Business Bank makes the same underlying distinction in its cash-flow guidance: rising profit does not prevent a shortage of cash when growth requires working capital.

Price the timing as well as the product

Payment terms are part of a commercial offer, not a minor line for finance to discover after the sale. If winning a contract requires financing the customer for longer, make that cost visible alongside gross margin and acquisition cost.

Using the illustration, an assumed annual funding cost of 10% on the additional £395,000 would be about £39,500 a year. That rate is a modeling assumption, not a financing quote. Fees, eligibility, concentration limits and the available facility could change the actual cost substantially.

The answer need not be a higher headline price. A setup fee payable before work starts, milestone billing or a deposit may reduce the amount financed. These are commercial options to negotiate, not terms every enterprise buyer will accept. They must fit the product and the customer’s purchasing process.

An early-payment discount also has a cost. Compare that cost against the cash released and the number of days gained, rather than assuming that faster payment is always worth any discount. The aim is to win a contract that the company can afford to deliver.

Check the customer’s record, not just its policy

Sixty-day terms and late payment are not the same thing. A customer paying exactly on day 60 has used the agreed credit period. A customer paying on day 75 has introduced another 15 days of uncertainty.

For many large UK companies, founders can check published payment-practices reports through the government’s reporting service. The reports show measures including average time to pay and the proportion of payments not made on time. Check the contracting legal entity, not merely the group’s familiar brand name.

Those reports are evidence to question, not a guarantee about one invoice. A company-wide average may not describe the startup’s business unit or contract. Use the information to ask concrete questions before signing: when does the clock start, which purchase-order details are mandatory, who accepts delivery and what happens if an invoice is rejected?

Ask the sales team to resolve those questions while the customer still wants the contract signed. Otherwise, an apparent 60-day deal may include weeks of avoidable administration before the agreed period even begins.

Do not fund growth with an assumed recovery

Keep a distinction between invoices expected to pay normally and overdue balances whose timing is uncertain. Repeated promises should not become fresh, certain cash dates in the board forecast.

For a UK receivable that has genuinely become overdue, establish whether the issue is administrative, a dispute or an inability to pay. Reconcile the balance and set a decision point for seeking local collection or legal advice, whether directly or through a platform such as Debitura. That is a recovery decision, not a substitute for funding the next month’s operating costs. Neither an instruction to collect nor a legal claim makes the money immediately available.

The useful board conversation comes before a cash crisis: how much growth can current liquidity support if customers take the time already allowed in their contracts? Run a second version with plausible delays and identify the point at which hiring or delivery commitments would need to change.

A prestigious customer can be a good investment. But its logo does not pay wages. The payment terms belong in the funding plan on the day the contract is evaluated, not on the day the first invoice goes overdue.

Swedish VC firm BackingMinds has received around €20 million from the European Investment Fund (EIF) for BackingMinds Invest III in order to seek out promising entrepreneurs and businesses often overlooked by traditional investors.

The EIF, which is part of the Luxembourg-based European Investment Bank (EIB) Group, will be the first institutional investor in the fund – backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme. This follows their €50 million fund close in 2022 and its investment in Swedish entrepreneurship platform Techarena in 2025.

“The future is never where you expect it, and neither are the founders building it,” says BackingMinds Founding Partner Sara Wimmercranz. “Some of the most innovative companies in the Nordics are being built where venture capital rarely reaches. A network is a filter. It lets through what already looks like the network and repeats the patterns of the past. As investors, we need to be more open and seek founders out. The EIF’s commitment lets us do that on a larger scale.”

BackingMinds’ EIF commitment comes amid further institutional backing for specialised European venture funds in 2026.

In Sweden, Norrsken Evolve closed a €62 million pre-Seed fund, while Turbine Capital reached a €54 million final close for Nordic DeepTech investments, both with EIF backing.

Elsewhere, Berlin-based Auxxo closed its €33.3 million Female Catalyst Fund II, Copenhagen’s Climentum Capital secured a €60 million first close for climate HardTech, including €40 million from the EIF, and Munich-based Ananda Impact Ventures raised €73 million at first close for impact investments.

Together, these fund closings represent approximately €282.3 million, excluding BackingMinds’ separate €20 million EIF commitment.

“Europe cannot afford to leave talented entrepreneurs undiscovered simply because they are outside the traditional venture capital networks,” adds EIF Deputy Chief Executive Merete Clausen. “BackingMinds has shown that promising businesses can be found in places and among founders that investors too often miss. By supporting this fund, we are helping to unlock that potential and bring more capital to companies tackling some of Europe’s most pressing challenges.”

Founded in 2016, BackingMinds is a Stockholm-based VC firm, founded by Sara Wimmercranz and Susanne Najafi to address the gaps in capital distribution. Through its two earlier funds, BackingMinds has invested in 23 companies.

Of these, 46% have had at least one female founder, 43% have had founders with immigrant backgrounds and 71% were established outside a capital city.

The new fund will finance early-stage companies primarily in Sweden and across the Nordic region, aiming to find entrepreneurial talent beyond established venture capital networks. It will seek out businesses founded by women as well as by people with immigrant backgrounds and based outside capital cities.

The focus will also be on commercially promising companies that address environmental or social challenges ranging from reducing carbon emissions and upgrading energy efficiency to improving healthcare and bolstering education.

According to the EIF, their support is aimed at helping BackingMinds Invest III attract other institutional investors.

 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {

}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor

 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {

 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {

}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {

 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.

 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}

 position: absolute;

 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {

 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }

 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {

 }
}

 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}

#sie-lead-form-drawer,

 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;

 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;

 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);

 border-top-left-radius: 22px;

 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {

 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;

 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;

 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;

 color: #0b3770;

 border-radius: 8px;

 flex-shrink: 0;

 }

 .sie-dest-panel__card {

 background: #1d3557;

 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );

 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,

 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>

</ul>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/internationalisation-at-the-university-of-helsinki" target="_blank">Internationalisation at the University of Helsinki </a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
                         <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q2.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/establishing-a-framework-of-inter-institutional-agreements-for-international-erasmus-mobility" target="_blank">Establishing a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for international Erasmus+ mobility</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/inter-institutional-agreements" target="_blank">Inter-Institutional Agreements</a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
                         <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-3.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">3</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q3.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution expresses its commitment to equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/ensuring-equal-access-and-opportunities-to-mobile-participants" target="_blank">Ensuring equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</a></div>

                                             </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">Before the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important for each HEI to produce an online Course Catalogue, which includes detailed, user-friendly and up-to-date information on the institution’s educational offer and learning environment to enable students to make the right choices and use their time most efficiently, before and during their study period.                          <p>Language preparation is a crucial element to ensure success in staff and student mobility outcomes. Both sending and receiving partners should agree on the recommended language level in the language of instruction/work of mobile students and staff. This level should be expressed according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR): <a href="https://europass.cedefop.europa.eu/en/resources/european-language-levels-cefr">https://europass.cedefop.europa.eu/en/resources/european-language-levels-cefr</a></p><p>The recommended language level should be agreed in the Inter-Institutional Agreement of the sending and receiving institutions for student mobility for studies. Similarly, a recommended language level should be agreed between the sending institution and the receiving organisation/enterprise for student mobility for traineeships, to ensure a proper integration of the trainee in the organisation/enterprise.                                                 <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support services and/or structures (e.g. by appointing a counsellor or officer for those target groups)</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>To ensure fair and equitable opportunities to all potential participants, including those from groups which are usually under-represented in mobility programmes (students or staff with special needs, students from lower socio-economic backgrounds, with family responsibilities or with part-time jobs, etc.), it is important for institutions to devise and publicise a system that actively promotes mobility opportunities to students from these groups and ensures that their needs can be supported and their privacy respected.</p><p>This may be supported by inviting all those applying to the mobility programme to disclose whether they belong to an under-represented group, so that appropriate support can be provided at the receiving organisation.</p><p>Targeted support services may include, but are not limited to:</p><ul><li>Appointing a counsellor or officer for these under-represented groups,</li><li>Developing and delivering courses and exams through specific learning and teaching approaches</li><li>Developing specific support services, e.g. for people with special needs. Incoming participants with special needs have the right to benefit from the same support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</li></ul>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Before the mobility, your institution has established formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to e.g. the use of Learning Agreements)</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The formal procedures for recognising student mobility should clearly and unambiguously set out the responsibilities of an appointed academic, who has the authority, on behalf of the appropriate academic body, to:</p><ul><li>Approve the Learning Agreements,</li><li>Exceptionally amend the Learning Agreements, and</li><li>Recognise the successfully completed activities, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams.</li></ul>                      </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">During the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> During the mobility, your institution fosters the integration of the incoming mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                                            </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides opportunities for incoming mobile participants to share their culture and experiences with their peers inside and with the local community</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Incoming mobile students also bring new perspectives to the institution, the local students and the culture which is part of the internationalisation of the receiving institution. This is a significant opportunity to benefit from the experiences that international students bring. To capitalise on these experiences, the institution and its student organisations should put in place opportunities for incoming students to showcase their talent and perspectives through access to existing local initiatives (e.g. school teaching programmes, community projects) and setting up new initiatives to celebrate the different cultures (e.g. theatre performances, food and cultural weeks etc.). Local associations can support the integration of incoming students with the local community, through existing initiatives such as the Social Erasmus and Erasmus in School projects (<a href="http://socialerasmus.esn.org">http://socialerasmus.esn.org</a>).&nbsp;</p><p>Some incoming students may even have been involved in the management or governance of their sending institutions and recognising this opportunity and involving incoming students in similar functions in the receiving institution such as in the student union (elected representative) or working groups dedicated to the voice of the international student.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>                      </div>
